title: CompTIA A+ Core 2
realWorldValue: The 220-1202 is the second of two exams required for the CompTIA A+ certification, focusing on operating systems, security, software troubleshooting, and operational procedures. Together with Core 1, it forms the long-standing entry credential for IT support roles — typical first certification for help desk technicians, field service engineers, and junior IT support staff.

skills: 1.1: Explain common operating system (OS) types and their purposes.
questions.question:
A graphic design studio is replacing several aging Windows machines and standardising on macOS for the creative team. The lead designer needs to share large project archives with external collaborators who use both Windows 11 laptops and older Windows 7 desktops. The studio wants a removable USB drive format that all three operating systems can read and write natively without installing extra drivers.

Which filesystem should the technician format the shared USB drive with?

choices.text: exFAT, because it is supported natively across modern Windows, macOS, and most Linux distributions for removable media.
choices.explanation: exFAT was designed by Microsoft for cross-platform removable storage and supports files larger than 4 GB.

choices.text: NTFS, because it gives the broadest cross-platform support for journaling and large files on portable media.
choices.explanation: macOS can read NTFS natively but cannot write to it without third-party drivers, so it fails the requirement.

choices.text: APFS, because it is optimised for solid-state storage and works on macOS and Windows alike.
choices.explanation: APFS is Apple-specific and is not natively readable by Windows without additional software.

choices.text: FAT32, because it is the most compatible format available for archives of any size.
choices.explanation: FAT32 is widely compatible but limits individual files to under 4 GB, which is unsuitable for large project archives.

questions.tip: Consider which filesystem balances cross-platform support with the ability to store very large individual files.
questions.explanation:
exFAT is the only format here that is natively read-write supported by Windows, macOS, and Linux on removable media while also supporting files larger than 4 GB.

**Why it works:** Microsoft licensed exFAT broadly so it is built into modern Windows and macOS, and most Linux distributions include it by default.

**Why the others don't work:**
- NTFS: macOS provides only read access without third-party drivers.
- APFS: Windows has no native support for APFS volumes.
- FAT32: 4 GB per-file limit blocks large project archives.

skills: 1.1: Explain common operating system (OS) types and their purposes.
questions.question:
During an asset refresh, the IT manager at a school is choosing low-cost devices for student use. The fleet must boot quickly, receive automatic updates from the vendor, run primarily web-based learning apps, and be centrally managed through a web console. Local storage needs are minimal because student files live in cloud storage.

Which workstation operating system best matches these requirements?

choices.text: Chrome OS, because it is built around web apps and is centrally manageable through the Google Admin console.
choices.explanation: Chrome OS targets thin-client style workloads, updates automatically, and supports enterprise enrolment for fleet management.

choices.text: Windows 11 Home, because it offers the widest application compatibility for school environments.
choices.explanation: Home edition cannot join a domain or be centrally managed by enterprise tools and is not optimised for thin devices.

choices.text: macOS, because it provides the most secure default configuration for shared student devices.
choices.explanation: macOS hardware is significantly more expensive and does not fit the low-cost, web-centric requirement.

choices.text: A community Linux distribution such as Ubuntu, because it gives the lowest licensing cost for student fleets.
choices.explanation: While inexpensive, a general Linux distribution lacks the unified cloud management console that the scenario requires.

questions.tip: Match the OS to a fleet that lives mostly in a browser and needs a vendor-managed console.
questions.explanation:
Chrome OS is purpose-built for low-cost, web-first devices that are managed centrally.

**Why it works:** Chromebooks ship with automatic vendor updates, fast boot, and integration with the Google Admin console for fleet policies.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Windows 11 Home: lacks domain join and central management features.
- macOS: hardware costs do not match a low-cost school deployment.
- Ubuntu: no unified vendor-managed console out of the box.

skills: 1.1: Explain common operating system (OS) types and their purposes.
questions.question:
The operations team is reviewing a list of workstations still running Windows 10 after the vendor announced its end-of-life date. Management asks the desktop team to explain the security implication of keeping the OS in production past that date. The team needs a concise answer that captures the primary risk rather than feature gaps.

Which consequence most accurately describes running an OS past its EOL date?

choices.text: The vendor stops issuing routine security updates, so newly discovered vulnerabilities will not be patched on those systems.
choices.explanation: EOL means the vendor no longer ships free security updates, leaving the OS exposed to new vulnerabilities.

choices.text: The OS will refuse to boot until a supported version is installed on the device.
choices.explanation: EOL does not disable the operating system; it simply ends update support.

choices.text: All installed applications will be blocked from running by the vendor's licensing servers.
choices.explanation: Vendors do not remotely disable third-party applications on EOL operating systems.

choices.text: The system will lose access to all local files until the user upgrades to a supported edition.
choices.explanation: Local files remain accessible after EOL; only update support ends.

questions.tip: Focus on what the vendor stops doing, not on what the OS itself stops doing.
questions.explanation:
An EOL operating system continues to run but no longer receives security patches, which is the primary risk.

**Why it works:** Without vendor patches, newly disclosed vulnerabilities accumulate and the attack surface grows over time.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Boot refusal: EOL does not disable the OS.
- App blocking: vendors do not police third-party app execution.
- File lockout: user data remains accessible.

skills: 1.1: Explain common operating system (OS) types and their purposes.
questions.question:
Following a hardware audit, a field technician is preparing to image a batch of Linux servers that will host a database workload. The senior engineer specifies a filesystem that is the default on Red Hat Enterprise Linux 8 and is tuned for very large files and high parallel I/O. The technician needs to pick the right filesystem during partitioning.

Which Linux filesystem matches this description?

choices.text: XFS, because it is the default on recent Red Hat Enterprise Linux releases and scales well for large files and concurrent I/O.
choices.explanation: XFS is RHEL's default and is well suited to large-file, high-throughput workloads.

choices.text: ext4, because it is the only journaling filesystem available on enterprise Linux.
choices.explanation: ext4 is a popular Linux filesystem but is not the default on modern RHEL and is not described as tuned for very large files.

choices.text: APFS, because it provides journaling and snapshots for Linux database hosts.
choices.explanation: APFS is Apple's filesystem and is not used as a Linux server filesystem.

choices.text: ReFS, because it is optimised for resilience on Linux database deployments.
choices.explanation: ReFS is a Microsoft filesystem for Windows Server, not a Linux option.

questions.tip: Match the filesystem to its default distribution and workload profile.
questions.explanation:
XFS is the default filesystem on modern Red Hat Enterprise Linux and is designed for high-throughput, large-file workloads.

**Why it works:** XFS uses extents and allocation groups that scale well under parallel I/O typical of database servers.

**Why the others don't work:**
- ext4: still common, but not the RHEL default and not the best fit for the described workload.
- APFS: Apple-only, not a Linux filesystem.
- ReFS: Microsoft-only, not a Linux filesystem.

skills: 1.1: Explain common operating system (OS) types and their purposes.
questions.question:
The IT lead at a small architecture firm is evaluating mobile devices for site visits. Staff want a tablet with a stylus, native support for the App Store ecosystem, and integration with macOS for handoff features such as continuity sketching. They also expect long vendor support for security updates.

Which TWO mobile operating systems are produced by Apple and offered on devices that fit this brief?

choices.text: iPadOS, which runs on iPad hardware and supports stylus input and continuity features with macOS.
choices.explanation: iPadOS is Apple's tablet OS and integrates with macOS Continuity features.

choices.text: iOS, which runs on iPhone hardware and shares the App Store and Apple ID ecosystem with iPadOS.
choices.explanation: iOS is Apple's phone OS and shares the App Store ecosystem with iPadOS.

choices.text: Android, which is the closest Apple equivalent and supports App Store integration.
choices.explanation: Android is developed by Google and uses the Play Store, not the App Store.

choices.text: Chrome OS, which Apple licenses for tablet hardware aimed at creative workflows.
choices.explanation: Chrome OS is a Google product for laptops and convertibles and is not licensed to Apple.

choices.text: Windows Mobile, which is currently shipped on Apple tablets with stylus support.
choices.explanation: Windows Mobile is a discontinued Microsoft OS and was never used on Apple hardware.

questions.tip: Identify which mobile platforms come from the same vendor as macOS.
questions.explanation:
Apple ships iPadOS on iPads and iOS on iPhones; both are built on the same foundation and integrate with macOS through Continuity.

**Why it works:** Both iOS and iPadOS share the App Store, Apple ID, and Continuity features that integrate with macOS.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Android: a Google platform with a different app store.
- Chrome OS: a Google laptop OS, not an Apple mobile OS.
- Windows Mobile: discontinued, never on Apple hardware.

questions.question: Match each filesystem to the operating system where it is most commonly used as a default or native option.

choices.text: Default filesystem for the system drive on Windows client editions
choices.explanation: NTFS is the standard Windows filesystem with journaling and ACL support.

choices.text: Default filesystem on modern macOS with native snapshot support
choices.explanation: APFS replaced HFS+ as the default macOS filesystem and is optimised for SSDs.

choices.text: Common default filesystem on many mainstream desktop Linux distributions
choices.explanation: ext4 is widely used as the default on distributions such as Ubuntu and Debian.

choices.text: Resilience-focused filesystem found on Windows Server storage workloads
choices.explanation: ReFS is designed for large, resilient storage workloads on Windows Server.

questions.tip: Pair each filesystem with the vendor that ships it as a default.
questions.explanation: Each of these filesystems is associated with a specific OS family: Windows clients use NTFS, Windows Server has ReFS for resilient storage, macOS uses APFS, and many desktop Linux systems default to ext4.

skills: 1.2: Given a scenario, perform OS installations and upgrades in a diverse environment.
questions.question:
During a hardware refresh, a technician is preparing a new workstation that ships with a 4 TB NVMe drive and UEFI firmware. The desktop team requires the system disk to support more than four primary partitions and a partition table that fully addresses the entire drive. The technician is at the partitioning step of the Windows 11 installer.

Which partition style should the technician select for the system disk?

choices.text: GPT, because it supports drives larger than 2 TB and allows many primary partitions.
choices.explanation: GPT works with UEFI, supports very large drives, and removes the four-primary-partition limit.

choices.text: MBR, because it is required by Windows 11 on UEFI systems for backward compatibility.
choices.explanation: MBR is limited to 2 TB and to four primary partitions, and Windows 11 on UEFI uses GPT.

choices.text: MBR with an extended partition to bypass the 2 TB address limit.
choices.explanation: Extended partitions allow more logical volumes but do not raise the MBR 2 TB total addressing limit.

choices.text: A dynamic disk in MBR mode to gain GPT-like behaviour without changing the table type.
choices.explanation: Dynamic disks are a separate Windows feature and do not lift MBR's size or primary-partition limits.

questions.tip: Match the partition table to a UEFI system with a drive larger than 2 TB.
questions.explanation:
GPT pairs with UEFI firmware and is required to fully use a 4 TB drive with many primary partitions.

**Why it works:** GPT uses 64-bit LBA addressing and allows up to 128 partitions on Windows by default.

**Why the others don't work:**
- MBR: 2 TB and four-primary-partition limits both apply.
- MBR with extended partition: does not raise the 2 TB total ceiling.
- Dynamic disk in MBR mode: does not change the underlying partition table limits.

skills: 1.2: Given a scenario, perform OS installations and upgrades in a diverse environment.
questions.question:
The desktop team is rolling out 80 identical laptops to a new contact centre. Each laptop must arrive with the same OS build, drivers, applications, and security baseline. The team wants the shortest hands-on time per device and is willing to invest in capturing a reference image.

Which installation method best fits this requirement?

choices.text: Image deployment, where a captured reference image is pushed to each device by a deployment server.
choices.explanation: Image deployment applies a single golden image across many identical devices, minimising per-device time.

choices.text: Clean install from USB on each device, followed by manual driver and application installation.
choices.explanation: Clean installs require significant hands-on time per device and do not guarantee a consistent baseline.

choices.text: Repair installation triggered from the recovery partition of each device.
choices.explanation: Repair installs are used to fix an existing OS, not to roll out new builds to many machines.

choices.text: In-place upgrade from the manufacturer image to the corporate build.
choices.explanation: An in-place upgrade preserves the existing OEM software and is slower than imaging for fleet deployments.

questions.tip: Pick the method that scales best when many devices share the same target build.
questions.explanation:
Image deployment is designed to roll out a single tested build across many identical machines.

**Why it works:** A reference image captures OS, drivers, apps, and policies at once, then deploys them in minutes per device.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Clean install from USB: high manual effort per machine.
- Repair install: meant for OS repair, not new deployments.
- In-place upgrade: keeps OEM cruft and is slower than imaging.

skills: 1.2: Given a scenario, perform OS installations and upgrades in a diverse environment.
questions.question:
Following a board approval to upgrade from Windows 10 to Windows 11, the helpdesk lead is drafting the pre-upgrade checklist. The lead wants to make sure that personal documents, settings, and bookmarks survive the transition for users who choose the in-place upgrade path.

Which consideration must the checklist include before starting the upgrades?

choices.text: Back up user files and preferences before starting any upgrade in case the process fails.
choices.explanation: Backups protect against upgrade failures that may leave the profile or files unusable.

choices.text: Switch every system disk from GPT to MBR before launching the upgrade.
choices.explanation: Windows 11 expects GPT on UEFI systems; changing to MBR would block installation.

choices.text: Disable BitLocker permanently on each device so the installer can write to the disk.
choices.explanation: BitLocker can be suspended for the upgrade and re-enabled afterwards; permanent disabling is unnecessary.

choices.text: Wipe each device first to ensure the upgrade behaves like a clean install.
choices.explanation: Wiping defeats the purpose of an in-place upgrade and removes user data the team wants to preserve.

questions.tip: Think about what protects user data when an upgrade goes wrong.
questions.explanation:
Backing up files and user preferences is the foundational safeguard before any in-place upgrade.

**Why it works:** If the upgrade fails, a recent backup restores the user's data and settings without rework.

**Why the others don't work:**
- GPT to MBR: Windows 11 on UEFI requires GPT.
- Permanently disabling BitLocker: only a temporary suspension is needed.
- Wiping the device: removes the data the upgrade is meant to preserve.

skills: 1.2: Given a scenario, perform OS installations and upgrades in a diverse environment.
questions.question:
A field technician is dispatched to reinstall Windows on a laptop that no longer boots. The internal drive is healthy, but the user has no installation media and a slow internet connection. The OEM enabled a vendor-supplied recovery partition on the drive when the device shipped.

Which installation method should the technician use first?

choices.text: Trigger an installation from the OEM recovery partition on the internal drive.
choices.explanation: A recovery partition lets the technician reinstall the factory OS without external media or large downloads.

choices.text: Perform an internet-based install over the user's home connection.
choices.explanation: Internet-based installation requires significant bandwidth that the scenario explicitly lacks.

choices.text: Boot a network installation from a corporate PXE server.
choices.explanation: A field laptop is not on the corporate network, so PXE is not available.

choices.text: Image deployment from a captured golden image stored on a USB drive.
choices.explanation: The technician has no installation media on hand, ruling out USB image deployment in this scenario.

questions.tip: Look for the method that needs nothing beyond what is already on the device.
questions.explanation:
The OEM recovery partition stores a vendor image that can reinstall the OS locally.

**Why it works:** It is already present on the internal drive and does not require media or bandwidth.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Internet-based install: slow connection blocks it.
- PXE network install: no corporate network present.
- USB image deployment: no installation media available.

skills: 1.2: Given a scenario, perform OS installations and upgrades in a diverse environment.
questions.question:
Midway through configuring a workstation for a CAD operator, the technician realises the new OS install requires third-party storage drivers that are not included with the Windows installer. The team wants to make sure these drivers are available during setup so that the installer can see the RAID volume and continue.

Which TWO actions are appropriate during the OS installation to handle this driver requirement?

choices.text: Download the vendor's RAID driver package and copy it to a USB drive that will be present during installation.
choices.explanation: Having the driver on removable media lets the installer load it on demand when the disk does not appear.

choices.text: Use the Load driver option in the Windows installer to point at the USB driver location.
choices.explanation: The installer's Load driver option imports third-party storage drivers so the RAID volume becomes visible.

choices.text: Skip the partitioning step and install Windows to the OS recovery partition instead.
choices.explanation: Installing onto a recovery partition is not a supported way to expose an unseen RAID volume.

choices.text: Switch the firmware from UEFI to legacy BIOS so the RAID volume becomes visible to the installer.
choices.explanation: Toggling firmware mode does not load third-party drivers and may break the existing GPT layout.

choices.text: Format the RAID volume with FAT32 from another machine before starting the install.
choices.explanation: Formatting elsewhere does not help if the installer cannot see the storage controller at all.

questions.tip: Focus on how the installer learns about hardware it does not recognise.
questions.explanation:
Third-party storage drivers are loaded by preparing them on removable media and then importing them through the installer's load driver step.

**Why it works:** The Windows installer accepts driver INF packages from USB media at the disk selection screen, exposing the RAID controller.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Installing to recovery partition: not a workaround for missing storage drivers.
- Switching firmware mode: does not provide drivers and may break the layout.
- Pre-formatting from another machine: cannot help if the controller is invisible.

skills: 1.2: Given a scenario, perform OS installations and upgrades in a diverse environment.
questions.question: Arrange the following clean-install steps in the correct order for a new Windows workstation that will boot from USB.

choices.text: Create bootable installation media on a USB drive using the vendor's media creation tool
choices.explanation: Bootable media must exist before the technician can start the installation.

choices.text: Configure the firmware to boot from the USB device and launch the installer
choices.explanation: Firmware boot order changes route the system to the installer on the USB drive.

choices.text: Select the partition style and create or format the system partition
choices.explanation: Partitioning prepares the disk to receive the OS files.

choices.text: Apply the OS image and complete out-of-box configuration including drivers and updates
choices.explanation: After the image is applied, the technician finalises drivers, updates, and user setup.

questions.tip: Think about what must exist before the next step is possible.
questions.explanation: A clean install begins with creating media, then booting from it, then preparing the disk, and finally applying the image and configuring the system.

skills: 1.3: Compare and contrast basic features of Microsoft Windows editions.
questions.question:
The operations team is reviewing a Windows 11 deployment plan for a finance department. Each workstation must join the corporate Active Directory domain, be managed by Group Policy, and have BitLocker enabled on the system drive. Cost is a concern, so the team wants the cheapest edition that meets every requirement.

Which Windows 11 edition should the team choose?

choices.text: Windows 11 Pro, because it supports domain join, Group Policy, and BitLocker out of the box.
choices.explanation: Pro is the lowest-tier edition that includes domain join, gpedit, and BitLocker.

choices.text: Windows 11 Home, because it includes BitLocker and can be added to a domain through a separate licence.
choices.explanation: Home cannot join an Active Directory domain regardless of additional licensing.

choices.text: Windows 11 Enterprise, because it is the only edition that supports Group Policy.
choices.explanation: Enterprise is more expensive and is not the only edition with Group Policy support.

choices.text: Windows 11 Education, because it is bundled with BitLocker and free for finance departments.
choices.explanation: Education is restricted to qualified institutions and is not generally available to finance departments.

questions.tip: Match the cheapest edition that includes domain join, gpedit, and BitLocker.
questions.explanation:
Windows 11 Pro is the entry point for domain join, Group Policy editing, and BitLocker.

**Why it works:** Pro includes all three required features and costs less than Enterprise.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Home: no domain join, no gpedit.
- Enterprise: meets the requirements but is more expensive than necessary.
- Education: not generally licensable to a finance department.

skills: 1.3: Compare and contrast basic features of Microsoft Windows editions.
questions.question:
During a workstation procurement review, an engineer is specifying machines for video editors who routinely load 256 GB of RAM and use server-class CPUs. Standard Pro hits a hard RAM limit that blocks the workload, so the team wants an edition designed for high-end client hardware without buying Enterprise volume licensing.

Which Windows 10 edition should the engineer specify?

choices.text: Windows 10 Pro for Workstations, because it raises the supported RAM ceiling and targets high-end client hardware.
choices.explanation: Pro for Workstations is specifically designed for high-memory, server-class client systems.

choices.text: Windows 10 Home, because it supports the highest RAM ceiling on consumer hardware.
choices.explanation: Home is capped at 128 GB of RAM and is unsuitable for high-memory client workloads.

choices.text: Windows 10 Pro standard, because it has no RAM ceiling and works on any client hardware.
choices.explanation: Standard Pro is capped at 2 TB of RAM in spec but does not include the workstation-class optimisations needed for ReFS and SMB Direct.

choices.text: Windows 10 Enterprise N, because it removes the RAM cap when sold without media features.
choices.explanation: N versions only remove certain media features and do not change RAM limits.

questions.tip: Pick the edition aimed at high-memory, server-class client hardware.
questions.explanation:
Pro for Workstations is the dedicated edition for power users with extreme hardware.

**Why it works:** It supports more RAM, ReFS, and persistent memory features tuned for workstation hardware.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Home: hard 128 GB cap.
- Pro standard: lacks workstation features.
- Enterprise N: N only removes media components.

skills: 1.3: Compare and contrast basic features of Microsoft Windows editions.
questions.question:
The procurement team has shortlisted laptops for a Windows 11 rollout. One model lacks a TPM 2.0 chip but otherwise has a fast CPU and plenty of RAM. The compliance lead asks whether the model can be used without firmware tricks or unsupported workarounds.

Which requirement does this laptop fail to meet?

choices.text: Windows 11 requires TPM 2.0 as a supported hardware prerequisite for installation.
choices.explanation: TPM 2.0 is part of Microsoft's published Windows 11 hardware requirements.

choices.text: Windows 11 requires legacy BIOS firmware rather than UEFI.
choices.explanation: Windows 11 requires UEFI with Secure Boot, not legacy BIOS.

choices.text: Windows 11 requires an MBR system disk for compatibility with older drivers.
choices.explanation: Windows 11 requires GPT on UEFI systems, not MBR.

choices.text: Windows 11 requires that the device be joined to a workgroup instead of a domain.
choices.explanation: Joining a workgroup is not a hardware requirement and has no bearing on supported install.

questions.tip: Recall the security chip Microsoft made a baseline for Windows 11.
questions.explanation:
TPM 2.0 is one of Microsoft's headline hardware requirements for Windows 11.

**Why it works:** TPM 2.0 enables secure key storage and is mandatory in the published requirements.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Legacy BIOS: Windows 11 needs UEFI.
- MBR system disk: Windows 11 needs GPT on UEFI.
- Workgroup join: unrelated to hardware support.

skills: 1.3: Compare and contrast basic features of Microsoft Windows editions.
questions.question:
A junior technician is troubleshooting a remote support request. The user runs Windows 11 Home and cannot enable inbound RDP for a vendor engineer to take over the desktop. The technician verifies the firewall, network, and credentials all look correct.

Which edition behaviour explains why inbound RDP is unavailable?

choices.text: Windows 11 Home does not include the inbound RDP host component; it can only act as an RDP client.
choices.explanation: RDP host support is reserved for Pro and higher editions.

choices.text: Windows 11 Home requires the user to join a domain before the RDP host service starts.
choices.explanation: Home cannot join a domain at all, and RDP host availability is determined by edition, not domain membership.

choices.text: Windows 11 Home limits RDP to incoming connections from devices on the same wireless subnet.
choices.explanation: There is no such subnet limitation on RDP; the issue is that the host service is not available.

choices.text: Windows 11 Home requires BitLocker to be enabled before RDP can accept inbound sessions.
choices.explanation: BitLocker is not a prerequisite for RDP and is not bundled with Home.

questions.tip: Recall which client editions can host RDP versus only connect out.
questions.explanation:
Home editions ship without the RDP host component, so inbound sessions are not possible.

**Why it works:** Microsoft reserves the RDP server role for Pro and higher editions.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Domain dependency: Home cannot join a domain, and that is not the gating factor.
- Subnet rule: no such restriction exists.
- BitLocker prerequisite: unrelated to RDP and unavailable on Home.

skills: 1.3: Compare and contrast basic features of Microsoft Windows editions.
questions.question:
The systems engineer is planning an upgrade path from Windows 10 Pro to Windows 11 Pro for a small accounting firm. The firm wants to keep installed applications, user profiles, and licensing intact, while ensuring the hardware can support the new OS.

Which TWO upgrade considerations apply to this in-place upgrade?

choices.text: Verify each device meets Windows 11 hardware requirements including TPM 2.0 and UEFI.
choices.explanation: Microsoft enforces hardware checks before allowing the upgrade to proceed.

choices.text: Confirm the upgrade path from Windows 10 Pro to Windows 11 Pro is supported as an in-place upgrade.
choices.explanation: Same-edition upgrades from Windows 10 to Windows 11 are supported, but cross-edition paths may not be.

choices.text: Reformat each system drive from GPT to MBR before launching the upgrade.
choices.explanation: Windows 11 requires GPT on UEFI systems, so this would block the upgrade.

choices.text: Force a clean install from USB for every device to bypass driver checks.
choices.explanation: A clean install would discard installed applications and profiles, which the firm wants to keep.

choices.text: Disable Secure Boot in firmware before starting the upgrade.
choices.explanation: Secure Boot is required for Windows 11; disabling it blocks the upgrade.

questions.tip: Focus on what supports an in-place upgrade rather than what bypasses it.
questions.explanation:
Supported in-place upgrades require both hardware compliance and a valid edition-to-edition path.

**Why it works:** Pro to Pro is a supported same-edition upgrade, and TPM 2.0 plus UEFI satisfy Microsoft's hardware gate.

**Why the others don't work:**
- GPT to MBR: breaks Windows 11 requirements.
- Forced clean install: discards profiles and apps the firm wants to keep.
- Disabling Secure Boot: blocks Windows 11 installation.

skills: 1.4: Given a scenario, use Microsoft Windows operating system features and tools.
questions.question:
The operations team is reviewing a workstation that crashes intermittently. The technician needs to read the recent system, application, and security logs to look for hardware warnings and service failures across the last 24 hours. The user has admin rights on the device.

Which Microsoft Management Console snap-in should the technician open?

choices.text: Event Viewer (`eventvwr.msc`), because it consolidates system, application, and security logs in one place.
choices.explanation: Event Viewer is the standard tool for reviewing Windows logs by category.

choices.text: Task Scheduler (`taskschd.msc`), because it shows recent scheduled task failures with the same timestamps.
choices.explanation: Task Scheduler focuses on scheduled jobs, not full system or application logs.

choices.text: Disk Management (`diskmgmt.msc`), because crashes often originate from volume and partition issues.
choices.explanation: Disk Management deals with volume layout, not log review.

choices.text: Local Users and Groups (`lusrmgr.msc`), because intermittent crashes correlate to local account changes.
choices.explanation: lusrmgr.msc manages local accounts and does not show system logs.

questions.tip: Match the snap-in to centralised log review.
questions.explanation:
Event Viewer is the single console for reading Windows logs across categories.

**Why it works:** It exposes system, application, security, and custom logs with filtering by source, level, and time.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Task Scheduler: scheduled tasks only.
- Disk Management: storage layout only.
- lusrmgr.msc: account management only.

skills: 1.4: Given a scenario, use Microsoft Windows operating system features and tools.
questions.question:
Following user complaints that a laptop is slow to log in, the helpdesk technician wants to identify which programs launch automatically when Windows starts and disable any unnecessary ones. The technician needs a built-in tool that shows the startup impact rating alongside each entry.

Which Task Manager tab should the technician use?

choices.text: The Startup tab, which lists auto-start applications and their impact rating.
choices.explanation: Task Manager's Startup tab is the dedicated place to manage and disable auto-start apps.

choices.text: The Services tab, which lists every background service and lets the technician disable startup behaviour.
choices.explanation: Services tab covers Windows services, not user-mode auto-start programs.

choices.text: The Performance tab, which charts CPU and memory under startup load.
choices.explanation: Performance shows live counters but does not list auto-start programs.

choices.text: The Users tab, which shows which user account triggers each auto-start entry.
choices.explanation: Users tab shows logged-in sessions, not startup item details.

questions.tip: Find the tab that names auto-start programs and their startup impact.
questions.explanation:
The Startup tab is purpose-built for listing and managing auto-start entries with their impact ratings.

**Why it works:** It exposes a one-click enable/disable for each entry along with the impact rating.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Services: background services, not user auto-start apps.
- Performance: live counters only.
- Users: session view, not startup items.

skills: 1.4: Given a scenario, use Microsoft Windows operating system features and tools.
questions.question:
During a hardware change, the technician needs to confirm whether a missing webcam is a driver problem or a hardware fault. The device should appear in the OS, but the technician wants to see the device tree, driver status, and any yellow warning icons.

Which built-in tool should the technician use?

choices.text: Device Manager (`devmgmt.msc`), because it shows the hardware tree with driver status and warning icons.
choices.explanation: Device Manager is the canonical tool for inspecting per-device driver state.

choices.text: System Information (`msinfo32.exe`), because it lists every webcam currently installed on the system.
choices.explanation: msinfo32 lists hardware but does not expose driver status or interactive troubleshooting.

choices.text: Performance Monitor (`perfmon.msc`), because it can graph the webcam's frame rate over time.
choices.explanation: perfmon does not surface driver health and is not used for missing-device troubleshooting.

choices.text: Resource Monitor (`resmon.exe`), because it correlates the webcam's I/O and CPU use.
choices.explanation: Resource Monitor shows resource usage by process, not device-level driver state.

questions.tip: Pick the snap-in that displays the device tree and driver state.
questions.explanation:
Device Manager exposes the device tree with driver state and warning icons.

**Why it works:** It allows updating, rolling back, disabling, and uninstalling drivers from the same view.

**Why the others don't work:**
- msinfo32: inventory only.
- perfmon: performance counters only.
- Resource Monitor: process-level resource usage only.

skills: 1.4: Given a scenario, use Microsoft Windows operating system features and tools.
questions.question:
A user reports the system drive is almost full on a Windows 11 laptop. The technician wants to reclaim space by removing temporary files, Windows update leftovers, and old Recycle Bin contents using a built-in utility designed for that purpose.

Which tool should the technician launch?

choices.text: Disk Cleanup (`cleanmgr.exe`), which can target temporary files, update leftovers, and Recycle Bin contents.
choices.explanation: Disk Cleanup is the built-in utility for clearing well-known categories of disposable files.

choices.text: Disk Defragmenter (`dfrgui.exe`), which compacts files to free space.
choices.explanation: Defragmenting reorganises files but does not free disk space.

choices.text: Registry Editor (`regedit.exe`), which can purge temp file entries.
choices.explanation: regedit modifies registry keys and is not used to delete files for space reclamation.

choices.text: Disk Management (`diskmgmt.msc`), which can shrink the system partition to make space available.
choices.explanation: Shrinking a partition does not delete junk files; it adjusts volume size only.

questions.tip: Pick the utility designed to delete known disposable file categories.
questions.explanation:
Disk Cleanup is the built-in tool for reclaiming space from known disposable categories.

**Why it works:** It enumerates safe-to-delete groups such as temp files, update artefacts, and Recycle Bin.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Defragmenter: does not free space.
- regedit: registry edits, not file deletion.
- Disk Management: volume layout, not file cleanup.

skills: 1.4: Given a scenario, use Microsoft Windows operating system features and tools.
questions.question:
The operations team is troubleshooting a workstation that fails to load several services after boot. The technician suspects an unwanted entry in the startup configuration and wants to compare service status with real-time CPU and disk usage to spot the offending process.

Which TWO tools should the technician open to investigate?

choices.text: System Configuration (`msconfig.exe`) to review and toggle services and boot options.
choices.explanation: msconfig exposes service and boot configuration, which is where rogue startup entries are managed.

choices.text: Resource Monitor (`resmon.exe`) to correlate CPU, disk, and network activity by process.
choices.explanation: Resource Monitor shows real-time per-process resource use, helping to identify the offending process.

choices.text: Registry Editor (`regedit.exe`) to delete the suspect service key by hand.
choices.explanation: Deleting service keys directly is risky and is not the appropriate diagnostic step at this stage.

choices.text: Disk Defragmenter (`dfrgui.exe`) to reorder files associated with the slow service.
choices.explanation: Defragmenting does not address startup or service problems.

choices.text: Certificate Manager (`certmgr.msc`) to verify the certificate of each startup service.
choices.explanation: Certificate Manager is unrelated to diagnosing startup or process resource problems.

questions.tip: Pair a configuration tool with a live diagnostics tool.
questions.explanation:
msconfig lets the technician inspect and toggle startup behaviour, while resmon surfaces live per-process resource use.

**Why it works:** Together they let the technician narrow down which startup entry is consuming resources or failing.

**Why the others don't work:**
- regedit: too invasive as a first step.
- Defragmenter: unrelated to startup issues.
- certmgr: certificate store, not process diagnostics.

skills: 1.4: Given a scenario, use Microsoft Windows operating system features and tools.
questions.question: Match each MMC snap-in to the administrative task it supports.

choices.text: Create, format, and resize volumes and partitions on local disks
choices.explanation: Disk Management handles volume layout, partitioning, and formatting.

choices.text: Create and manage scheduled jobs that run on triggers or timers
choices.explanation: Task Scheduler manages scheduled jobs that run on triggers or timers.

choices.text: Inspect, import, and export personal and trusted root certificates
choices.explanation: Certificate Manager lets users and admins inspect certificate stores.

choices.text: Edit local Group Policy settings on Pro and higher editions
choices.explanation: Group Policy Editor edits the local computer and user policy on supported editions.

questions.tip: Match each snap-in to the kind of object it manages.
questions.explanation: Each of these snap-ins manages a different administrative surface: disks, scheduled tasks, certificates, and local policy.

skills: 1.5: Given a scenario, use the appropriate Microsoft command-line tools.
questions.question:
During a network troubleshooting call, the helpdesk technician needs to view the IPv4 address, subnet mask, default gateway, and DNS servers configured on every adapter of a Windows workstation. The technician wants a single command that prints all of this information at once.

Which command should the technician run?

choices.text: `ipconfig /all` to display full adapter configuration including DNS servers.
choices.explanation: ipconfig /all extends the default output with DNS, DHCP, and MAC details.

choices.text: `ipconfig` with no switches, which already prints DNS for every adapter.
choices.explanation: Bare ipconfig shows IP, mask, and gateway but omits DNS server entries.

choices.text: `netstat -an` to list adapter addresses and DNS in one table.
choices.explanation: netstat lists connections and listening ports, not adapter configuration.

choices.text: `nslookup` to dump every DNS server registered on each adapter.
choices.explanation: nslookup queries DNS but does not show local adapter configuration.

questions.tip: Use the switch that extends adapter output to include DNS.
questions.explanation:
ipconfig /all prints the complete adapter configuration in a single shot.

**Why it works:** The /all switch adds DNS, DHCP lease, and MAC information to the default output.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Bare ipconfig: omits DNS servers.
- netstat -an: connections and ports, not adapter config.
- nslookup: DNS queries, not adapter config.

skills: 1.5: Given a scenario, use the appropriate Microsoft command-line tools.
questions.question:
After a domain admin updates a Group Policy that restricts removable storage, the user reports the policy has not taken effect. The technician wants to force the workstation to refresh both computer and user policy immediately without waiting for the next interval.

Which command should the technician run from an elevated prompt?

choices.text: `gpupdate /force` to reapply all Group Policy settings immediately.
choices.explanation: gpupdate /force reapplies all policy regardless of whether it has changed.

choices.text: `gpresult /r` to push the new policy to the workstation.
choices.explanation: gpresult reports the applied policy set; it does not refresh it.

choices.text: `sfc /scannow` to validate the policy files in the system store.
choices.explanation: sfc verifies system file integrity and is unrelated to policy refresh.

choices.text: `net use /persistent:yes` to map the policy share before reapplying it.
choices.explanation: net use maps shared drives; it does not refresh Group Policy.

questions.tip: Pick the command that forces Group Policy to reapply.
questions.explanation:
gpupdate /force triggers an immediate policy refresh without waiting for the next cycle.

**Why it works:** The /force flag reapplies all policy settings whether or not they have changed.

**Why the others don't work:**
- gpresult /r: reports applied policy only.
- sfc /scannow: file integrity scan.
- net use: drive mapping.

skills: 1.5: Given a scenario, use the appropriate Microsoft command-line tools.
questions.question:
A user reports their system feels unstable after a power loss. The technician wants to scan the system drive for filesystem errors and bad sectors, automatically repair any errors found, and recover readable information from bad sectors. The system drive is currently in use.

Which command should the technician schedule for the next reboot?

choices.text: `chkdsk C: /f /r` to fix errors and recover readable data from bad sectors.
choices.explanation: /f fixes errors found and /r locates bad sectors and recovers readable information.

choices.text: `chkdsk C: /x` to dismount the system drive and bypass the scan entirely.
choices.explanation: /x forces dismount but does not by itself fix errors or scan for bad sectors.

choices.text: `format C: /q` to clear the system drive and rebuild the filesystem.
choices.explanation: format would destroy data; it is not a repair tool for in-use system drives.

choices.text: `diskpart` to delete and recreate the system partition from scratch.
choices.explanation: diskpart manipulates partition layout; it does not repair filesystem errors.

questions.tip: Combine the switches that both fix errors and check sectors.
questions.explanation:
chkdsk with /f and /r both repairs filesystem errors and surveys the disk for bad sectors.

**Why it works:** /f writes corrections to the filesystem while /r reads every sector and recovers readable data.

**Why the others don't work:**
- chkdsk /x: dismount only.
- format /q: destructive.
- diskpart: partition layout, not repair.

skills: 1.5: Given a scenario, use the appropriate Microsoft command-line tools.
questions.question:
The operations team is migrating a project folder from a retiring file server to a new one. The technician needs a tool that copies the directory tree, preserves NTFS permissions, mirrors deletions, and can retry transient network failures during the long copy.

Which command-line tool should the technician use?

choices.text: `robocopy` with mirror and retry options to preserve attributes and ACLs.
choices.explanation: robocopy is designed for resilient large copies with mirroring and ACL preservation.

choices.text: `xcopy` with the `/y` overwrite switch to copy the folder tree.
choices.explanation: xcopy lacks the resiliency and mirroring features that robocopy provides for large transfers.

choices.text: `md` to create the destination tree and then drag-and-drop the files in File Explorer.
choices.explanation: md only creates directories and File Explorer is not appropriate for resumable, ACL-preserving transfers.

choices.text: `format` to wipe the new server volume before mounting the share.
choices.explanation: format is destructive and does not copy files.

questions.tip: Pick the modern tool built for resilient, attribute-preserving copies.
questions.explanation:
robocopy is the standard Windows tool for robust file replication.

**Why it works:** It preserves attributes and ACLs, retries on failure, and supports mirroring.

**Why the others don't work:**
- xcopy: weaker resiliency, fewer attribute options.
- md plus Explorer: not designed for migration workloads.
- format: destructive, irrelevant.

skills: 1.5: Given a scenario, use the appropriate Microsoft command-line tools.
questions.question:
Following a user complaint about a slow website, the helpdesk technician wants to confirm DNS resolution works correctly and trace the path packets take to the destination. The technician needs to identify whether the slowness is local or somewhere along the route.

Which TWO commands should the technician run?

choices.text: `nslookup` to verify the domain resolves to an expected IP address.
choices.explanation: nslookup confirms whether the local DNS resolver returns a valid record.

choices.text: `tracert` to map each hop between the workstation and the destination.
choices.explanation: tracert shows the hops on the route, helping locate where latency is introduced.

choices.text: `netstat -ano` to list every listening port on the destination web server.
choices.explanation: netstat reports local connection state, not remote routing or DNS resolution.

choices.text: `chkdsk /f` to repair the local DNS resolver cache.
choices.explanation: chkdsk fixes filesystem errors and is unrelated to DNS or routing.

choices.text: `sfc /scannow` to verify that the resolver service binaries are intact.
choices.explanation: sfc validates system files but does not diagnose DNS or path issues.

questions.tip: Pair a DNS check with a route trace.
questions.explanation:
Confirming DNS resolution and mapping the route to the destination are the right first two checks for a slow site complaint.

**Why it works:** nslookup verifies the name maps to a sensible address, and tracert highlights the hop where latency is introduced.

**Why the others don't work:**
- netstat: local connection state.
- chkdsk: filesystem repair.
- sfc: system file integrity.

skills: 1.5: Given a scenario, use the appropriate Microsoft command-line tools.
questions.question: Match each Windows command-line tool to the task it performs.

choices.text: Print the computer name of the local system
choices.explanation: hostname returns the local computer's NetBIOS or DNS host name.

choices.text: Show the user account currently signed in to the session
choices.explanation: whoami prints the current user identity.

choices.text: Show the installed Windows version in a dialog box
choices.explanation: winver opens a small About Windows dialog with version details.

choices.text: Combine ping and traceroute behaviour to measure loss at each hop
choices.explanation: pathping samples each hop on a route to identify packet loss locations.

questions.tip: Match each command to a small, distinct function it performs.
questions.explanation: These tools return identity, version, and network diagnostic information in small focused ways.

skills: 1.6: Given a scenario, configure Microsoft Windows settings.
questions.question:
The operations team is preparing laptops for sales staff who travel frequently. The team wants to make sure that closing the lid puts the device into sleep mode while on battery, but does nothing while on AC power so users can dock without interrupting external displays.

Which Settings area should the technician use to apply this behaviour?

choices.text: Power Options, which exposes Choose what closing the lid does for each power state.
choices.explanation: Power Options exposes the lid-close action separately for battery and AC power.

choices.text: Devices and Printers, which lists each laptop's lid sensor as a controllable device.
choices.explanation: Devices and Printers manages hardware devices but does not configure lid-close behaviour.

choices.text: Personalization, which controls screen behaviour when the lid closes.
choices.explanation: Personalization deals with themes and visuals, not power events.

choices.text: Indexing Options, which manages the laptop's sleep index for fast wake.
choices.explanation: Indexing Options controls search indexing, not sleep behaviour.

questions.tip: Pair the setting that handles lid action with the right Settings panel.
questions.explanation:
Power Options is where the lid-close action is configured per power state.

**Why it works:** It separates settings for battery and plugged-in modes, supporting the requested behaviour.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Devices and Printers: device inventory only.
- Personalization: themes, not power.
- Indexing Options: search indexing only.

skills: 1.6: Given a scenario, configure Microsoft Windows settings.
questions.question:
A user reports they cannot see configuration files in a project directory because Windows is hiding them. The technician needs to enable display of hidden items and stop hiding extensions of common file types so the user can see and edit the configuration files safely.

Which Windows Settings or Control Panel area should the technician open?

choices.text: File Explorer Options, which has toggles for hidden items and known file extensions.
choices.explanation: File Explorer Options has the View tab with hidden file and extension toggles.

choices.text: Indexing Options, which controls whether hidden files are visible in File Explorer.
choices.explanation: Indexing Options controls search indexing, not visibility of hidden files.

choices.text: Administrative Tools, which exposes hidden files for support staff.
choices.explanation: Administrative Tools is a launcher for snap-ins, not for File Explorer visibility settings.

choices.text: Privacy settings, which masks file extensions until the user grants permission.
choices.explanation: Privacy controls app permissions, not file visibility.

questions.tip: Find the dialog that controls hidden files and extensions.
questions.explanation:
File Explorer Options is the canonical place to enable hidden items and unhide extensions.

**Why it works:** The View tab exposes both toggles in a single window.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Indexing Options: search-related only.
- Administrative Tools: snap-in launcher.
- Privacy: app permission settings.

skills: 1.6: Given a scenario, configure Microsoft Windows settings.
questions.question:
The security team has flagged that inbound RDP must remain blocked on user laptops, except for a single jump host that the helpdesk operates. The technician needs to allow RDP from one specific source IP while continuing to block all other inbound RDP traffic.

Which Windows Settings area should the technician use?

choices.text: Windows Defender Firewall with Advanced Security, which supports scoped rules by source address.
choices.explanation: Advanced Firewall rules can be scoped to specific remote IP ranges per port and program.

choices.text: Internet Options, which can whitelist source IPs for inbound RDP traffic.
choices.explanation: Internet Options configures the legacy Internet Explorer security zones, not firewall rules.

choices.text: Network and Sharing Center, which has a panel for inbound RDP exceptions.
choices.explanation: Network and Sharing Center exposes adapter info and sharing, not granular firewall rules.

choices.text: User Accounts, which can restrict RDP to specific source addresses per user.
choices.explanation: User Accounts manages local accounts, not firewall scoping.

questions.tip: Choose the firewall area that allows scoping by remote IP.
questions.explanation:
Windows Defender Firewall with Advanced Security supports scoping inbound rules by remote address.

**Why it works:** Advanced rules let the technician specify which remote IP ranges are allowed for a given port and program.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Internet Options: legacy browser zones, not firewall.
- Network and Sharing Center: shared device info, no granular rules.
- User Accounts: account management, not firewall.

skills: 1.6: Given a scenario, configure Microsoft Windows settings.
questions.question:
A user reports a printer that no longer responds. The technician suspects the queued documents are stuck. The technician wants to view the print queue, cancel pending jobs, and verify printer status from a single Control Panel page.

Which Control Panel area should the technician use?

choices.text: Devices and Printers, which lists installed printers and exposes the queue for each.
choices.explanation: Devices and Printers is the standard location to interact with installed printers and queues.

choices.text: Programs and Features, which lists printer drivers as installed programs.
choices.explanation: Programs and Features lists installed software, not active print queues.

choices.text: Sound, which previews printer status notifications.
choices.explanation: Sound configures audio playback, not printer queues.

choices.text: Mail, which dispatches print jobs over Outlook.
choices.explanation: Mail configures Outlook profiles, not printer queues.

questions.tip: Pick the panel that lists installed printers and queues.
questions.explanation:
Devices and Printers is the central panel for installed printers and queues.

**Why it works:** Right-click on a printer to see queue, status, and properties.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Programs and Features: installed software only.
- Sound: audio settings only.
- Mail: Outlook profile settings only.

skills: 1.6: Given a scenario, configure Microsoft Windows settings.
questions.question:
The operations team is preparing a Windows 11 device for a user who travels with a mobile hotspot. The team wants to make sure that large Windows Updates do not consume the user's cellular data while tethered, but normal updates resume when the user returns to home Wi-Fi.

Which TWO settings should the technician configure?

choices.text: Mark the hotspot connection as a metered connection in Network and Internet settings.
choices.explanation: Metered connections cause Windows Update to defer large downloads to conserve data.

choices.text: Confirm that the home Wi-Fi connection is not flagged as metered so updates flow normally.
choices.explanation: Leaving the home network unmetered ensures updates resume when the user is back on Wi-Fi.

choices.text: Disable all Windows Updates from the Update and Security panel entirely.
choices.explanation: Disabling updates leaves the device unpatched and contradicts the requirement to resume updates on Wi-Fi.

choices.text: Switch the device to airplane mode whenever using the hotspot.
choices.explanation: Airplane mode disables radios entirely and blocks the user's connectivity.

choices.text: Configure a proxy server in Internet Options to compress all hotspot traffic.
choices.explanation: Internet Options does not control Windows Update behaviour by data plan.

questions.tip: Use the per-network metered flag to control Windows Update bandwidth.
questions.explanation:
Marking the hotspot as metered and leaving home Wi-Fi unmetered gives Windows Update the right context to choose when to download.

**Why it works:** Windows Update respects the metered flag and defers large downloads accordingly.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Disabling updates entirely: contradicts the requirement.
- Airplane mode: blocks all connectivity.
- Proxy in Internet Options: not relevant to update bandwidth control.

skills: 1.6: Given a scenario, configure Microsoft Windows settings.
questions.question: Match each Windows Settings or Control Panel area to the configuration task it supports.

choices.text: Change desktop background, accent colours, themes, and lock screen images
choices.explanation: Personalization controls visual settings and themes.

choices.text: Set the system clock, time zone, keyboard layout, and display language
choices.explanation: Time and Language covers locale, time zone, and keyboard settings.

choices.text: Enable narrator, magnifier, high contrast themes, and other accessibility aids

choices.text: Manage Windows Update settings, backup, and recovery options

skills: 1.7: Given a scenario, configure Microsoft Windows networking features on a client/desktop.
questions.question:
The operations team is migrating a small office from a workgroup to an Active Directory domain. The team wants centrally managed user accounts, shared drives that follow each user across machines, and printers that anyone in the domain can install with one click.

Which change does joining the domain provide that the workgroup setup did not?

choices.text: Centralised authentication and policy through a domain controller for users and devices.
choices.explanation: Domain join authenticates and applies policy through the domain controller for every member device.

choices.text: Automatic conversion of every local profile into a workgroup-wide account.
choices.explanation: Domain join does not transform existing local profiles; it adds domain accounts alongside them.

choices.text: A built-in VPN tunnel between every workstation and the home network.
choices.explanation: Domain join does not establish VPN tunnels.

choices.text: Permanent disabling of the local administrator account on every member machine.
choices.explanation: Local admin accounts remain after domain join; behaviour is controlled by policy, not removal.

questions.tip: Focus on what a domain provides that a workgroup cannot.
questions.explanation:
Domain join provides centralised authentication and policy via the domain controller.

**Why it works:** Users and devices authenticate against the directory and inherit Group Policy.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Auto-conversion of profiles: not a function of domain join.
- Built-in VPN: not a feature of domain join.
- Disabling local admin: not automatic on domain join.

skills: 1.7: Given a scenario, configure Microsoft Windows networking features on a client/desktop.
questions.question:
A user at a coffee shop reports they cannot reach corporate web apps even though the Wi-Fi shows connected. The technician sees the connection is flagged as a public network. The team wants a secure way to reach internal resources from any untrusted network without exposing them to the public.

Which connection type should the technician configure on the laptop?

choices.text: A VPN connection that tunnels traffic to the corporate network over the Wi-Fi link.
choices.explanation: A VPN creates an encrypted tunnel between the client and the corporate network.

choices.text: Switch the Wi-Fi network from public to private to expose the corporate apps.
choices.explanation: Changing the profile does not bridge the laptop to internal resources.

choices.text: Configure a proxy in Internet Options to forward all traffic to the corporate firewall.
choices.explanation: A proxy alone does not provide secure access to internal resources from a public network.

choices.text: Enable file and printer sharing on the public network profile.
choices.explanation: Sharing on public networks exposes the laptop to untrusted devices without solving the access need.

questions.tip: Choose the connection that securely extends the corporate network to the device.
questions.explanation:
A VPN connection is the standard way to access corporate resources from public networks.

**Why it works:** Traffic is encrypted and tunnelled to a corporate gateway that grants access to internal services.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Public to private switch: changes firewall behaviour, not connectivity.
- Proxy only: not a substitute for tunnelled access.
- File and printer sharing on public: insecure and irrelevant.

skills: 1.7: Given a scenario, configure Microsoft Windows networking features on a client/desktop.
questions.question:
Following an office reorganisation, a workstation needs a fixed IP so a network printer can find it reliably. The technician is at the IPv4 properties page for the wired adapter and must enter four values to complete the static configuration.

Which set of fields must the technician populate?

choices.text: IP address, subnet mask, default gateway, and preferred DNS server.
choices.explanation: These four fields are the standard static IPv4 configuration on a Windows client.

choices.text: IP address, MAC address, broadcast address, and proxy server.
choices.explanation: MAC and broadcast are not entered manually on the IPv4 properties page; proxy is configured separately.

choices.text: Hostname, workgroup name, user PIN, and BitLocker recovery key.
choices.explanation: None of these fields are part of the IPv4 properties page.

choices.text: DHCP scope, lease length, reservation MAC, and router admin password.
choices.explanation: These are DHCP server-side fields, not client static configuration values.

questions.tip: Recall the four fields required to make a Windows client static IPv4 configuration complete.
questions.explanation:
Static IPv4 configuration on Windows requires an address, subnet mask, gateway, and at least one DNS server.

**Why it works:** These four fields let the system address the network, route off-subnet, and resolve names.

**Why the others don't work:**
- MAC/broadcast/proxy: not part of static IPv4 fields.
- Hostname/workgroup/PIN/BitLocker key: unrelated.
- DHCP server fields: not entered on the client.

skills: 1.7: Given a scenario, configure Microsoft Windows networking features on a client/desktop.
questions.question:
A user wants quick access to a department share at \\fs01\projects on a domain-joined workstation. The technician wants a persistent mapping that survives reboots and appears as a drive letter in File Explorer.

Which approach should the technician take?

choices.text: Use Map Network Drive in File Explorer pointing to the UNC path with Reconnect at sign-in enabled.
choices.explanation: Map Network Drive creates a persistent drive letter that reconnects on sign-in.

choices.text: Create a shortcut on the desktop that points at the UNC path.
choices.explanation: A shortcut does not provide a drive letter in File Explorer.

choices.text: Add the UNC path to Internet Options as a trusted site.
choices.explanation: Internet Options does not mount network drives.

choices.text: Configure a static route to the file server in the routing table.
choices.explanation: Routing table entries do not create drive mappings.

questions.tip: Pick the feature that creates a persistent drive letter from a UNC path.
questions.explanation:
Map Network Drive creates a persistent letter mapped to a UNC path.

**Why it works:** The Reconnect at sign-in option restores the mapping on every login.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Desktop shortcut: no drive letter.
- Trusted site: browser-only.
- Static route: routing, not mapping.

skills: 1.7: Given a scenario, configure Microsoft Windows networking features on a client/desktop.
questions.question:
Midway through troubleshooting, the technician discovers a user's laptop cannot reach any internal sites by name, although it can ping internal IPs. The team suspects DNS, gateway, or a stale lease on the wired adapter. The user has admin rights and a wired connection.

Which TWO actions are the most useful starting points?

choices.text: Verify that the configured DNS server addresses are correct for the corporate network.
choices.explanation: Wrong or missing DNS servers explain why names fail but IPs work.

choices.text: Release and renew the DHCP lease to ensure the laptop has current settings.
choices.explanation: A fresh DHCP lease refreshes IP, gateway, and DNS in one step.

choices.text: Disable the firewall entirely so all DNS replies can return.
choices.explanation: Disabling the firewall is unsafe and does not address typical DNS resolution problems.

choices.text: Switch the laptop's network profile from private to public to flush DNS caches.
choices.explanation: Profile changes do not clear or fix DNS resolution.

choices.text: Configure a manual proxy server pointing at the internal site addresses.
choices.explanation: Configuring a proxy does not resolve a DNS lookup problem.

questions.tip: Focus on configuration values that explain why names fail but IPs work.
questions.explanation:
Confirming DNS settings and refreshing the DHCP lease are the right first steps for symptomatic name-resolution failures.

**Why it works:** Either step exposes or corrects the most likely root causes for a DNS-specific failure.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Disabling firewall: unsafe and unrelated to DNS misconfiguration.
- Profile change: does not affect resolution.
- Proxy configuration: not a DNS fix.

skills: 1.7: Given a scenario, configure Microsoft Windows networking features on a client/desktop.

skills: 1.8: Explain common features and tools of the macOS/desktop operating system.
questions.question:
The operations team is preparing macOS laptops for designers who carry confidential client briefs. The team needs to encrypt the system drive so that data is protected if a laptop is lost or stolen, using a built-in macOS feature with no third-party software.

Which macOS feature should the team enable?

choices.text: FileVault, which provides full-disk encryption for the macOS system volume.
choices.explanation: FileVault is Apple's built-in full-disk encryption feature for macOS.

choices.text: Time Machine, which encrypts backups and the system drive together.
choices.explanation: Time Machine handles backups; the system-drive encryption is a separate feature.

choices.text: Keychain, which stores encrypted credentials and protects the system volume.
choices.explanation: Keychain stores passwords and certificates but does not encrypt the disk.

choices.text: Spotlight, which encrypts indexed content on the system drive.
choices.explanation: Spotlight is a search index, not an encryption feature.

questions.tip: Match the macOS feature for full-disk encryption to its name.
questions.explanation:
FileVault is the built-in macOS full-disk encryption feature.

**Why it works:** It encrypts the system volume using a recovery key tied to the user account.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Time Machine: backups, not disk encryption.
- Keychain: credential storage only.
- Spotlight: search indexing only.

skills: 1.8: Explain common features and tools of the macOS/desktop operating system.
questions.question:
A user wants to quickly find a file, calculator result, and weather forecast without opening individual apps on macOS. The user prefers a single keystroke that opens a system-wide search bar from anywhere in the OS.

Which macOS feature should the user learn?

choices.text: Spotlight, which provides system-wide search from a keystroke.
choices.explanation: Spotlight indexes the system and offers quick answers, calculations, and file search.

choices.text: Mission Control, which surfaces files and previews from any desktop.
choices.explanation: Mission Control shows open windows and desktops, not a search bar.

choices.text: Finder, which opens a window to browse files manually.
choices.explanation: Finder is a file browser, not a system-wide quick search.

choices.text: Keychain, which surfaces files and contacts by keyword.
choices.explanation: Keychain stores credentials and is not a search tool.

questions.tip: Pick the macOS feature designed for instant system-wide search.
questions.explanation:
Spotlight is the canonical system-wide search on macOS.

**Why it works:** It indexes files, settings, and many third-party data sources and offers quick calculations and conversions.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Mission Control: window switcher.
- Finder: manual file browser.
- Keychain: credential store.

skills: 1.8: Explain common features and tools of the macOS/desktop operating system.
questions.question:
A user reports an application is unresponsive on macOS and the spinning wait cursor persists. The technician wants to terminate just that app without affecting other running applications or signing the user out.

Which macOS feature should the technician use?

choices.text: Force Quit on the unresponsive application.
choices.explanation: Force Quit terminates the chosen application without affecting other apps or the session.

choices.text: Restart the Mac from the Apple menu to clear the hang.
choices.explanation: A restart affects every running app and the user's session.

choices.text: Log out the user and sign back in to release the hung process.
choices.explanation: Logging out is more disruptive than necessary for a single hung app.

choices.text: Open Disk Utility and run First Aid on the system disk.
choices.explanation: Disk Utility checks storage; it does not stop hung applications.

questions.tip: Choose the action that targets only the misbehaving application.
questions.explanation:
Force Quit terminates only the hung application.

**Why it works:** It exits the chosen process while leaving other apps and the session intact.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Restart: too disruptive.
- Log out: still disruptive.
- Disk Utility: storage tool, not process control.

skills: 1.8: Explain common features and tools of the macOS/desktop operating system.
questions.question:
A designer wants to back up a MacBook to an external SSD on a rolling schedule so that previous file versions can be restored. The designer prefers a built-in macOS backup tool that supports incremental snapshots without paying for extra software.

Which tool should the designer use?

choices.text: Time Machine targeting the external SSD as the backup destination.
choices.explanation: Time Machine is the built-in incremental backup tool for macOS.

choices.text: Disk Utility to clone the internal volume to the external SSD nightly.
choices.explanation: Disk Utility can clone but does not provide rolling incremental snapshots.

choices.text: Finder to drag the home folder to the external SSD periodically.
choices.explanation: Manual drag-and-drop is not incremental and does not retain previous versions.

choices.text: Keychain to back up application data to the external SSD.
choices.explanation: Keychain stores credentials and is not a backup tool.

questions.tip: Pick the macOS feature designed for incremental snapshot backups.
questions.explanation:
Time Machine is the built-in incremental backup feature for macOS.

**Why it works:** It creates rolling snapshots so previous file versions can be restored from any point.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Disk Utility clone: full clone, not rolling history.
- Finder copy: manual and non-versioned.
- Keychain: credential store only.

skills: 1.8: Explain common features and tools of the macOS/desktop operating system.
questions.question:
The IT team is rolling out a new internal application on macOS workstations. They want to use installation file formats native to macOS that staff can launch from a download without any third-party tools.

Which TWO macOS installation file types should the team distribute?

choices.text: A `.pkg` installer that runs a guided installation through Installer.
choices.explanation: .pkg is the standard macOS installer format and runs without extra tools.

choices.text: A `.dmg` disk image that contains the application bundle for drag-and-drop install.
choices.explanation: .dmg is the typical distribution format on macOS for app bundles.

choices.text: An `.msi` Windows installer that staff can extract with a converter.
choices.explanation: .msi is a Windows format and is not native to macOS.

choices.text: An `.exe` Windows binary that staff can run after enabling a compatibility layer.
choices.explanation: .exe is a Windows binary and is not native to macOS.

choices.text: A bare folder of source code that staff can compile themselves.
choices.explanation: Source compilation is not a standard macOS distribution mechanism for end users.

questions.tip: Pick the formats macOS opens natively without third-party software.
questions.explanation:
.pkg and .dmg are the two standard macOS installer formats.

**Why it works:** Both open natively in macOS without requiring extra tools.

**Why the others don't work:**
- .msi and .exe: Windows formats.
- Source folder: not an end-user format.

skills: 1.8: Explain common features and tools of the macOS/desktop operating system.
questions.question: Match each macOS system folder to its typical contents.
