skills: 1.9: Identify common features and tools of the Linux client/desktop operating system.
questions.question:
A junior technician is given a Linux workstation and asked to change the permissions on a script so that the owner can read, write, and execute it, while the group and others can only read and execute it. The technician is in the directory that holds the script.

Which command sets these permissions?

choices.text: `chmod 755 script.sh` to apply the requested permission set.
choices.explanation: 755 maps to rwx for owner and r-x for group and others.

choices.text: `chmod 777 script.sh` to grant the requested permission set.
choices.explanation: 777 also grants write to group and others, which is more permissive than requested.

choices.text: `chmod 644 script.sh` to grant the requested permission set.
choices.explanation: 644 omits execute, so the script could not be run by anyone.

choices.text: `chown 755 script.sh` to grant the requested permission set.
choices.explanation: chown changes ownership, not numeric permissions.

questions.tip: Map the rwx pattern to its three-digit octal form.
questions.explanation:
755 sets rwx for the owner and r-x for group and others.

**Why it works:** It matches the requested permission set exactly.

**Why the others don't work:**
- 777: too permissive.
- 644: no execute bit.
- chown: wrong tool.

skills: 1.9: Identify common features and tools of the Linux client/desktop operating system.
questions.question:
During an audit, the system administrator needs to install a new web server package on a Debian-based Linux workstation. The administrator wants to use the distribution's standard package manager and fetch from the configured repositories.

Which command should the administrator run?

choices.text: `sudo apt install nginx` to install from the configured repositories.
choices.explanation: apt is the standard package manager on Debian-based distributions.

choices.text: `sudo dnf install nginx` to install from the configured repositories.
choices.explanation: dnf is used on Red Hat-based distributions, not Debian-based ones.

choices.text: `sudo systemctl install nginx` to install the service binaries.
choices.explanation: systemctl manages services; it does not install packages.

choices.text: `sudo mount install nginx` to attach the package to the system.
choices.explanation: mount attaches filesystems; it is not a package manager.

questions.tip: Pair the package manager with its distribution family.
questions.explanation:
apt is the standard package manager on Debian and Ubuntu.

**Why it works:** It resolves dependencies and installs from the configured repositories.

**Why the others don't work:**
- dnf: for Red Hat-based distributions.
- systemctl: service control, not installation.
- mount: filesystem operation.

skills: 1.9: Identify common features and tools of the Linux client/desktop operating system.
questions.question:
A user reports that an application log is growing rapidly and the technician suspects a particular error string is appearing many times. The technician needs to filter all lines that contain the string FAILED from the log file located at /var/log/app.log.

Which command should the technician run?

choices.text: `grep FAILED /var/log/app.log` to print all matching lines.
choices.explanation: grep filters lines that match a pattern from a file.

choices.text: `find FAILED /var/log/app.log` to list the matching lines.
choices.explanation: find locates files by name and attributes; it does not search file content.

choices.text: `cat FAILED /var/log/app.log` to display the matches.
choices.explanation: cat concatenates files; it does not filter by content.

choices.text: `mv FAILED /var/log/app.log` to extract the matches into a new file.
choices.explanation: mv renames or moves files; it does not search.

questions.tip: Pick the standard Linux tool for content filtering in files.
questions.explanation:
grep is the standard tool for searching file content for a pattern.

**Why it works:** It prints every line in the file that matches the supplied pattern.

**Why the others don't work:**
- find: filename search, not content.
- cat: display, not filter.
- mv: rename or move files.

skills: 1.9: Identify common features and tools of the Linux client/desktop operating system.
questions.question:
The operations team needs to mount a new NFS share automatically every time a Linux workstation boots. The administrator wants the change to survive reboots without scripting and to be declarative.

Which configuration file should the administrator edit?

choices.text: `/etc/fstab` to add a persistent mount entry for the NFS share.
choices.explanation: fstab defines filesystems that are mounted at boot.

choices.text: `/etc/resolv.conf` to add the NFS server's DNS records and mount line.
choices.explanation: resolv.conf configures DNS resolution, not mount entries.

choices.text: `/etc/passwd` to add the NFS mount as a user shell entry.
choices.explanation: passwd holds user account data, not mount entries.

choices.text: `/etc/hosts` to register the NFS share as a static hostname-to-mount mapping.
choices.explanation: hosts maps hostnames to IP addresses; it does not mount filesystems.

questions.tip: Pick the file that lists filesystems mounted at boot.
questions.explanation:
/etc/fstab is the declarative table of filesystems mounted at boot.

**Why it works:** Each line describes a device, mount point, type, and options that systemd applies at boot.

**Why the others don't work:**
- /etc/resolv.conf: DNS resolver settings.
- /etc/passwd: user accounts.
- /etc/hosts: name-to-IP mappings.

skills: 1.9: Identify common features and tools of the Linux client/desktop operating system.
questions.question:
A junior analyst has flagged that a Linux workstation feels slow and the technician wants quick insight into running processes, CPU and memory use, and free disk space without installing any extra tools.

Which TWO commands should the technician use?

choices.text: `top` to view live process activity and resource usage.
choices.explanation: top shows running processes with CPU and memory consumption in real time.

choices.text: `df` to view free space on each mounted filesystem.
choices.explanation: df reports filesystem usage.

choices.text: `mv` to relocate processes between cores for better performance.
choices.explanation: mv moves files; it does not affect processes.

choices.text: `chmod` to lower permissions on heavy processes.
choices.explanation: chmod changes permissions; it does not show process or disk data.

choices.text: `curl` to display CPU and memory summary from a remote endpoint.
choices.explanation: curl transfers data over the network and is not a system status tool.

questions.tip: Pair a process tool with a disk-usage tool.
questions.explanation:
top surfaces live process and resource data while df shows disk usage by filesystem.

**Why it works:** Together they answer both halves of the slowness question.

**Why the others don't work:**
- mv: file moves.
- chmod: permissions.
- curl: network transfer.

skills: 1.9: Identify common features and tools of the Linux client/desktop operating system.
questions.question: Match each Linux command or component to its purpose.

choices.text: Change the user or group that owns a file or directory

skills: 1.10: Given a scenario, install applications according to requirements.
questions.question:
The procurement team is evaluating a new 3D rendering application for the design studio. The vendor publishes minimum requirements that include a dedicated GPU with 8 GB of VRAM and a 64-bit OS. The existing workstations have integrated graphics with shared memory and run 64-bit Windows.

Which requirement makes these workstations unsuitable for the new application?

choices.text: The workstations lack a dedicated GPU with the required VRAM.
choices.explanation: Integrated graphics share system memory and do not satisfy the dedicated VRAM requirement.

choices.text: The 64-bit OS prevents the application from using the GPU at all.
choices.explanation: 64-bit Windows is fully compatible with modern GPUs; the OS bitness is not the gating factor.

choices.text: The vendor's installer requires a 32-bit OS to access integrated graphics.
choices.explanation: Modern 3D applications do not require a 32-bit OS.

choices.text: Integrated graphics block all OpenGL features needed by 3D applications.
choices.explanation: Integrated graphics support OpenGL; the issue is dedicated VRAM, not API support.

questions.tip: Compare the workstation's hardware to the vendor's specific GPU and VRAM line.
questions.explanation:
The dedicated GPU and VRAM requirement is the failing constraint.

**Why it works:** Integrated graphics rely on shared system memory and cannot satisfy a dedicated VRAM requirement.

**Why the others don't work:**
- 64-bit OS as blocker: 64-bit is what the vendor wants.
- 32-bit requirement: outdated and unrelated.
- OpenGL block: integrated GPUs do support OpenGL.

skills: 1.10: Given a scenario, install applications according to requirements.
questions.question:
The operations team plans to roll out a new line-of-business application to 120 workstations on the same evening. The installer comes as an ISO file with several gigabytes of payload, and the team wants to avoid each workstation downloading the full file from the vendor.

choices.text: Host the ISO on a corporate share and mount it on each workstation for installation.
choices.explanation: A mounted ISO from a local share avoids per-workstation downloads from the vendor.

choices.text: Have each user download the installer from the vendor portal directly.
choices.explanation: Per-workstation downloads consume bandwidth and time exactly as the team wants to avoid.

choices.text: Email the ISO as an attachment to each user.
choices.explanation: Multi-gigabyte attachments are impractical and most mail systems reject them.

choices.text: Burn the ISO to a DVD and ship a copy to each desk.
choices.explanation: Physical media is slow to distribute and clashes with a same-evening rollout target.

questions.tip: Pick the method that scales to many devices on the same network.
questions.explanation:
A central mountable ISO on a corporate share is the right distribution model.

**Why it works:** Workstations install from the same local source, saving bandwidth and time.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Vendor downloads: high WAN cost.
- Email attachments: impractical.
- DVD shipments: too slow.

skills: 1.10: Given a scenario, install applications according to requirements.

The application has an external hardware token requirement.

skills: 1.10: Given a scenario, install applications according to requirements.

skills: 1.10: Given a scenario, install applications according to requirements.
questions.question:
The operations team is preparing to install a new accounting application that has both 32-bit and 64-bit versions. The estate is a mix of Windows 10 32-bit and Windows 11 64-bit workstations. skills: 1.10: Given a scenario, install applications according to requirements.

skills: 1.11: Given a scenario, install and configure cloud-based productivity tools.
questions.question:

Identity synchronisation links the on-premises directory to the cloud tenant.

skills: 1.11: Given a scenario, install and configure cloud-based productivity tools.
questions.question:

skills: 1.11: Given a scenario, install and configure cloud-based productivity tools.
questions.question:
A user wants their cloud storage folder to be available offline on their laptop so they can edit files on a long flight, with changes uploaded once the laptop reconnects. The administrator needs to choose the right client-side setting.

questions.tip: Match the sync setting that allows offline edits and later upload.

Folder sync with offline files is the right configuration.

**Why it works:** It caches files locally and reconciles changes upon reconnection.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Email workaround: no reconciliation.
- Read-only: blocks edits.
- Network drive without caching: unusable offline.

skills: 1.11: Given a scenario, install and configure cloud-based productivity tools.
questions.question:
Following a feedback session, the operations team is consolidating tools so staff have a single place for spreadsheets, word processing, and videoconferencing. The administrator wants to deploy a productivity suite that bundles these collaboration tools through the cloud tenant.

Which tool category is the administrator deploying?

questions.question:
The IT team is rolling out a cloud productivity tenant for a small charity. The team wants smooth collaboration features for remote staff and a way to make sure their corporate identities stay in sync between the on-premises directory and the cloud tenant.

Which TWO configuration steps should the team perform?

choices.text: Enable identity synchronisation from the on-premises directory to the cloud tenant.
choices.explanation: Identity sync mirrors accounts from the directory to the tenant.

choices.text: Assign licences to users so they can access email, storage, and collaboration tools.
choices.explanation: Licences are required for users to access cloud services.

choices.text: Disable all collaboration tools so users only use email.
choices.explanation: Disabling collaboration tools contradicts the rollout goal.

choices.text: Delete every directory account and recreate them in the cloud tenant.
choices.explanation: Deleting and recreating loses history and contradicts directory sync.

choices.text: Replace the corporate directory with a personal cloud login for each user.
choices.explanation: Personal cloud logins break central identity management.

questions.tip: Pair sync with licence assignment to bring users online.
questions.explanation:
Identity sync plus licence assignment together enable corporate users to access the tenant.

**Why it works:** Sync brings the identities across and licences open service access.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Disabling collaboration: contradicts the goal.
- Deleting and recreating: loses history and identity.
- Personal cloud logins: breaks central identity.

skills: 2.1: Summarize various security measures and their purposes.
questions.question:
The operations team is planning the entry layout for a new data centre lobby. They need a controlled space that prevents tailgating by trapping one person at a time between two interlocking doors, requiring badge verification before the inner door releases.

Which physical security control matches this requirement?

choices.text: Access control vestibule with interlocking doors and badge reader at the inner door.
choices.explanation: An access control vestibule (mantrap) physically prevents tailgating by allowing only one authenticated person through at a time.

choices.text: Bollards across the lobby entrance combined with motion sensors above the reception desk.
choices.explanation: Bollards block vehicles, not people; motion sensors only detect movement and do not prevent tailgating.

choices.text: A magnetometer at the main door paired with video surveillance covering the reception desk.
choices.explanation: Magnetometers detect metal and cameras only record; neither physically prevents a second person from following an authorised one.

choices.text: A standard door lock with a security guard performing periodic walkthroughs of the lobby.
choices.explanation: A guard walking by occasionally cannot enforce one-person-at-a-time entry on every badge swipe.

questions.tip: Focus on which control physically isolates one person between two doors.
questions.explanation:
An access control vestibule provides the interlocking-door behaviour described, gating entry on successful badge verification.

**Why it works:** The vestibule (mantrap) only releases the inner door after the outer door has closed and the badge has been verified, preventing tailgating by design.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Bollards target vehicles, not pedestrian piggybacking
- Magnetometers and cameras detect or record but do not block entry
- A periodic guard patrol cannot enforce single-entry on every badge swipe

skills: 2.1: Summarize various security measures and their purposes.
questions.question:
During an access review, the security team finds that several junior helpdesk technicians can read confidential HR records even though their job requires only password reset rights. The team wants to apply the foundational logical security model that grants users only the access strictly needed for their role.

Which principle should they apply?

choices.text: Principle of least privilege, restricting helpdesk accounts to the password reset operations they require.
choices.explanation: Least privilege grants only the minimum permissions needed to perform a role, removing unnecessary access.

choices.text: Zero Trust network segmentation that places HR file shares behind a separate VLAN with no firewall rules.
choices.explanation: Zero Trust is about continuous verification; simply VLAN-isolating shares with no rules does not address user permissions.

choices.text: Single sign-on so that one credential controls access to both helpdesk tools and HR records.
choices.explanation: SSO simplifies authentication but does not reduce what each account is authorised to read.

choices.text: Mandatory multifactor authentication on every helpdesk login to HR systems.
choices.explanation: MFA strengthens authentication but does not change the authorisation scope of the account.

questions.tip: Look for the control that limits authorisation rather than authentication.
questions.explanation:
Least privilege is the model that limits each account's permissions to exactly what the role needs.

**Why it works:** Removing HR read rights from helpdesk accounts aligns access with job duties and shrinks the impact of credential compromise.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Zero Trust segmentation without rules does not actually restrict authorised users
- SSO addresses identity convenience, not over-permissioned accounts
- MFA hardens login but leaves existing excessive permissions intact

skills: 2.1: Summarize various security measures and their purposes.
questions.question:
A finance manager is being onboarded to a cloud expenses platform. The identity team wants her to authenticate to the company's identity provider once, then have the expenses platform trust an XML-based assertion of her identity without prompting her to log in again.

Which standard performs this federated authentication exchange?

choices.text: Security Assertions Markup Language used to pass signed identity assertions between the identity provider and the expenses application.
choices.explanation: SAML is the XML-based standard used to federate identity between an IdP and a service provider.

choices.text: RADIUS sending an Access-Accept response from the identity provider to the expenses application.
choices.explanation: RADIUS is used for network access authentication, not browser-based federation between web applications.

choices.text: Kerberos tickets issued by the corporate domain controller for the expenses website.
choices.explanation: Kerberos is the on-prem domain authentication protocol and is not the federation standard described.

choices.text: A TOTP one-time code generated by the manager's authenticator app and submitted to the expenses application.
choices.explanation: TOTP is a second factor for login, not a federation assertion protocol.

questions.tip: Identify which standard delivers signed XML identity assertions across web applications.
questions.explanation:
SAML is the XML-based federation standard used for browser-based SSO between identity providers and service providers.

**Why it works:** The identity provider issues a signed SAML assertion that the expenses application trusts, so the user does not log in again.

**Why the others don't work:**
- RADIUS is for network-edge authentication (Wi-Fi, VPN)
- Kerberos is on-premises domain authentication, not web SSO federation
- TOTP is a one-time second factor, not a federation protocol

skills: 2.1: Summarize various security measures and their purposes.
questions.question:
The security team has flagged that domain administrators currently hold their elevated rights 24 hours a day. They want a model where admins request elevation only when needed, approval is granted for a short window, and the rights expire automatically afterward.

Which approach satisfies this requirement?

choices.text: Just-in-time access through a privileged access management platform that grants elevation for a defined time window.
choices.explanation: JIT via PAM grants elevation on demand for a fixed duration and revokes it automatically.

choices.text: Single sign-on so admins authenticate once and retain elevated rights across all administrative consoles.
choices.explanation: SSO simplifies repeated logins but does not time-bound elevated rights.

choices.text: An access control list applied to each server granting the admin group permanent full control.
choices.explanation: Permanent ACL entries are the opposite of time-bound elevation.

choices.text: Mobile device management policies pushing administrator credentials to managed laptops on demand.
choices.explanation: MDM manages devices and configuration, not on-demand role elevation.

questions.tip: Look for the control that issues short-lived, on-demand elevation.
questions.explanation:
Just-in-time access through PAM grants elevation only when requested and revokes it after a defined window.

**Why it works:** Standing privileges are removed, and admins request a short elevation window which the PAM platform enforces and audits.

**Why the others don't work:**
- SSO does not bound how long elevated rights last
- A permanent ACL leaves rights in place indefinitely
- MDM governs devices, not privileged role lifecycle

skills: 2.1: Summarize various security measures and their purposes.
questions.question:
A regional bank is rolling out multifactor authentication for its online banking customers. Compliance requires that the second factor be tied to something the user has and cannot be trivially intercepted by a SIM swap or call-forwarding attack against their phone number.

Which TWO factor types satisfy this requirement?

choices.text: A hardware security token that generates codes locally on the device.
choices.explanation: A hardware token's secret never traverses the carrier network, so it is immune to SIM swap.

choices.text: A TOTP code from an authenticator application on the customer's smartphone.
choices.explanation: TOTP codes are generated locally from a shared secret and do not rely on SMS or voice delivery.

choices.text: An SMS text message containing a one-time code sent to the registered mobile number.
choices.explanation: SMS codes are vulnerable to SIM swap and call-forwarding fraud.

choices.text: An automated voice call that reads out a one-time passcode to the registered mobile number.
choices.explanation: Voice calls share the same SIM swap and forwarding risks as SMS.

choices.text: An email containing a one-time code sent to the customer's primary email address.
choices.explanation: Email is a knowledge or possession factor depending on context, but it is not bound to a possessed device and can be compromised via account takeover.

questions.tip: Consider which factors keep the secret on a device the user physically holds.
questions.explanation:
Hardware tokens and authenticator-app TOTP both keep the shared secret on a possessed device and do not rely on the carrier network.

**Why it works:** Both methods generate codes locally, so they cannot be intercepted by porting a phone number or forwarding calls.

**Why the others don't work:**
- SMS codes can be redirected by SIM swap attacks
- Voice call delivery shares the same telephony weakness
- Email codes can be intercepted via inbox compromise and are not bound to a possessed device

skills: 2.1: Summarize various security measures and their purposes.
questions.question: Match each biometric authentication method to the physical trait it measures.

choices.text: Unique blood vessel patterns at the back of the eye
choices.explanation: Retina scans use near-infrared light to map vasculature on the inner eye.

choices.text: Ridge and valley patterns on a finger pad
choices.explanation: Fingerprint readers capture and compare friction ridge minutiae.

choices.text: Geometric measurements of facial landmarks captured by a camera
choices.explanation: FRT compares facial geometry such as eye spacing and nose-to-chin ratios.

choices.explanation: Voice biometrics compares speech samples against an enrolled voiceprint.
