questions.explanation: Each biometric method captures a different physical or behavioural trait using different sensors and matching algorithms.

skills: 2.2: Given a scenario, configure and apply basic Microsoft Windows OS security settings.
questions.question:
The IT lead at a small architecture firm needs to encrypt the entire C: volume of staff laptops so that data is unreadable if a laptop is stolen and the drive is removed. The laptops all have a TPM 2.0 chip, and recovery keys must be escrowed centrally.

Which Windows feature should be configured?

choices.text: BitLocker Drive Encryption on the system volume, with the recovery key backed up to the directory service.
choices.explanation: BitLocker uses the TPM to encrypt the whole volume and supports central recovery-key escrow.

choices.text: Encrypting File System applied to every user folder on the C: drive.
choices.explanation: EFS encrypts individual files or folders per user, not the entire system volume.

choices.text: NTFS Deny Read permissions on the C: drive root for the Everyone group.
choices.explanation: NTFS permissions only apply while Windows is running; removing the drive bypasses them.

choices.text: BitLocker-To-Go applied to the internal C: drive of each laptop.
choices.explanation: BitLocker-To-Go is for removable drives, not the system volume.

questions.tip: Identify the feature that encrypts the OS volume and uses the TPM.
questions.explanation:
BitLocker is the Windows full-volume encryption feature that uses the TPM and supports centrally escrowed recovery keys.

**Why it works:** The volume is encrypted at rest, and removal of the drive yields ciphertext that cannot be read without the TPM or recovery key.

**Why the others don't work:**
- EFS only protects selected files per user account
- NTFS permissions are bypassed once the drive is mounted elsewhere
- BitLocker-To-Go targets removable media, not the system volume

skills: 2.2: Given a scenario, configure and apply basic Microsoft Windows OS security settings.
questions.question:
A shared folder hosts a project plan on a Windows file server. The share permissions for the Project group are set to Change, but the underlying NTFS permissions grant the same group only Read. A user from the Project group connects across the network and tries to edit the file.

What effective access will the user have?

choices.text: Read only, because the most restrictive of the share and NTFS permissions applies when accessing across the network.
choices.explanation: Effective network access is the intersection of share and NTFS permissions; the most restrictive wins.

choices.text: Change, because the share permission is evaluated first and grants modify rights.
choices.explanation: Share permissions are not evaluated alone; NTFS still restricts the final access.

choices.text: Full Control, because Change at the share level always implies Full Control at the file system.
choices.explanation: Change does not imply Full Control, and NTFS still applies separately.

choices.text: No access, because conflicting share and NTFS permissions cause access to be denied by default.
choices.explanation: Conflicts resolve to the most restrictive granted right, not a denial.

questions.tip: When share and NTFS permissions differ over the network, consider which one wins.
questions.explanation:
Across the network, effective access is the intersection of share and NTFS permissions, so the user gets Read.

**Why it works:** Windows evaluates both ACLs; the more restrictive of the two becomes the effective permission for network access.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Share permissions do not override NTFS
- Change does not escalate to Full Control
- A mismatch does not automatically deny access; the lesser right is granted

skills: 2.2: Given a scenario, configure and apply basic Microsoft Windows OS security settings.
questions.question:
A standard user on a Windows 11 workstation needs to install a printer driver that requires elevated rights. The user is not in the local Administrators group, and the helpdesk wants to allow the installation to proceed without permanently elevating the account.

Which built-in mechanism allows the standard user to complete this task with administrator credentials?

choices.text: User Account Control prompts for an administrator credential when the elevated action is attempted.
choices.explanation: UAC's over-the-shoulder prompt accepts admin credentials to elevate a single action for a standard user.

choices.text: Adding the user temporarily to the Power Users group for the duration of the installation.
choices.explanation: Power Users is a legacy group with no meaningful elevated rights on modern Windows.

choices.text: Enabling the built-in Guest account so the installer runs without UAC prompts.
choices.explanation: The Guest account has fewer rights than a standard user and would not install drivers.

choices.text: Disabling UAC for the session so the installer runs without prompts.
choices.explanation: Disabling UAC weakens system security and does not grant the standard user admin rights.

questions.tip: Look for the built-in elevation prompt mechanism.
questions.explanation:
UAC presents an elevation prompt that accepts admin credentials, letting the standard session perform a single elevated action.

**Why it works:** The standard user does not gain persistent admin rights; only the requested install runs elevated after credentials are entered.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Power Users on modern Windows has no useful elevation
- The Guest account has fewer rights, not more
- Disabling UAC removes a control and still does not grant rights

skills: 2.2: Given a scenario, configure and apply basic Microsoft Windows OS security settings.
questions.question:
A domain administrator wants the Finance department's workstations to receive a stricter password policy and a specific desktop wallpaper, while leaving other departments untouched. The Finance computer accounts are already collected in a dedicated organizational unit.

Which Active Directory configuration should be applied?

choices.text: Link a Group Policy Object with the desired settings to the Finance organizational unit.
choices.explanation: Linking a GPO to an OU applies the settings only to objects within that OU.

choices.text: Edit the Default Domain Policy to include the Finance-specific password and wallpaper settings.
choices.explanation: Default Domain Policy applies to all domain members and would affect every department.

choices.text: Add the Finance computers to a global security group and apply NTFS permissions on the domain controller.
choices.explanation: NTFS permissions on a DC do not push wallpaper or password settings to workstations.

choices.text: Create a logon script on each Finance laptop that sets a registry key for the wallpaper.
choices.explanation: A local script per laptop is unmanaged, does not enforce the password policy, and bypasses centralised control.

questions.tip: Identify the scope that targets only one OU without affecting the whole domain.
questions.explanation:
Linking a GPO to the Finance OU applies the policy only to objects within that OU.

**Why it works:** Group Policy inheritance lets administrators target settings precisely at an OU without affecting peers in other OUs.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Default Domain Policy is domain-wide and over-broad
- NTFS permissions on a DC do not deploy desktop settings
- Per-machine scripts are unmanaged and do not cover the password policy

skills: 2.2: Given a scenario, configure and apply basic Microsoft Windows OS security settings.
questions.question:
A technician is hardening a Windows 11 workstation that has been running with default settings. Management wants confirmation that the built-in malware and network protections are both active and up to date before the laptop is issued to an executive traveller.

Which TWO actions should the technician take?

choices.text: Confirm Microsoft Defender Antivirus is enabled and run a definitions update.
choices.explanation: Active real-time protection plus current definitions is the baseline for built-in malware defence.

choices.text: Confirm Windows Defender Firewall is on for the Domain, Private, and Public profiles.
choices.explanation: All three profiles must be on so the firewall protects the laptop on any network it joins.

choices.text: Disable the built-in firewall while travelling so VPN traffic is not inspected.
choices.explanation: The firewall does not block legitimate VPN client traffic; disabling it removes a critical control.

choices.text: Add the user to the local Administrators group so they can update definitions on the road.
choices.explanation: Granting local admin rights weakens hardening and is not needed for automatic definition updates.

choices.text: Replace Defender Antivirus by uninstalling it before deploying a third-party suite.
choices.explanation: Defender cannot be uninstalled and is automatically suspended when an active third-party AV registers itself.

questions.tip: Consider the baseline malware and network controls that should be verified before release.
questions.explanation:
Verifying Defender Antivirus is active with current definitions and that the firewall is on for all profiles establishes the built-in hardening baseline.

**Why it works:** Both controls ship with Windows and provide the first line of defence against malware and unsolicited network traffic on any network the laptop joins.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Disabling the firewall removes essential protection on untrusted networks
- Local admin rights are not required for definition updates
- Defender cannot be cleanly uninstalled and is managed automatically

skills: 2.2: Given a scenario, configure and apply basic Microsoft Windows OS security settings.
questions.question: Match each Windows encryption or sign-in feature to the scenario it best addresses.

choices.text: Encrypts a removable USB flash drive so it cannot be read on an unauthorised PC
choices.explanation: BitLocker-To-Go is designed for removable media.

choices.text: Encrypts an individual user's files on an NTFS volume tied to their account certificate
choices.explanation: EFS encrypts specific files or folders for the logged-on user.

choices.text: Lets a user sign in using facial recognition or a fingerprint on supported hardware
choices.explanation: Windows Hello is the biometric passwordless sign-in feature.

choices.text: Authenticates the user with a device-specific numeric code held by the TPM
choices.explanation: A Windows PIN is bound to the device's TPM and is not transmitted off the machine.

questions.tip: Distinguish full-volume encryption from per-file encryption, and biometric sign-in from PIN sign-in.
questions.explanation: Each feature targets a different protection or authentication scenario in Windows.

skills: 2.3: Compare and contrast wireless security protocols and authentication methods.
questions.question:
The operations team is replacing a legacy SOHO router that currently advertises an open SSID. They want the strongest standardised consumer wireless protection that uses Simultaneous Authentication of Equals to resist offline dictionary attacks against the pre-shared key.

Which wireless protocol should they enable?

choices.text: WPA3 Personal, which uses SAE to negotiate the session key.
choices.explanation: WPA3 introduced SAE specifically to defeat offline dictionary attacks on the PSK.

choices.text: WPA2 Personal with TKIP for backwards compatibility.
choices.explanation: WPA2 with TKIP is the weakest WPA2 mode and is vulnerable to known attacks.

choices.text: WEP with a 128-bit key and shared-key authentication.
choices.explanation: WEP is broken and trivially crackable in minutes.

choices.text: An open SSID with MAC address filtering as the only access control.
choices.explanation: MAC filtering is easily bypassed by spoofing and leaves traffic unencrypted.

questions.tip: Look for the protocol that names SAE in its handshake.
questions.explanation:
WPA3 Personal uses SAE in place of the WPA2 4-way handshake to defeat offline PSK dictionary attacks.

**Why it works:** SAE negotiates a fresh, mutually authenticated key per session, so a captured handshake cannot be brute-forced offline.

**Why the others don't work:**
- WPA2 with TKIP keeps a deprecated cipher and remains vulnerable to capture-and-crack
- WEP encryption is broken
- MAC filtering provides no confidentiality and is bypassed by spoofing

skills: 2.3: Compare and contrast wireless security protocols and authentication methods.
questions.question:
A network engineer is migrating an office Wi-Fi network from WPA2 to a configuration that still uses WPA2 but replaces the older stream cipher with the recommended block cipher for confidentiality and integrity.

Which cipher should be configured?

choices.text: AES in CCMP mode as the WPA2 data cipher.
choices.explanation: CCMP/AES is the recommended WPA2 cipher and replaces TKIP.

choices.text: TKIP because it is the only cipher WPA2 supports for backwards compatibility.
choices.explanation: TKIP is the legacy WPA option retained for WPA2 compatibility but is not the recommended choice.

choices.text: RC4 used with a 104-bit key and a 24-bit initialisation vector.
choices.explanation: RC4 with a 24-bit IV describes WEP, not a WPA2 mode.

choices.text: 3DES in CBC mode running over the 4-way handshake.
choices.explanation: 3DES is not used by 802.11 data encryption; WPA2 uses AES-CCMP.

questions.tip: Recall which block cipher WPA2 introduced as the recommended replacement for TKIP.
questions.explanation:
AES with CCMP is the recommended WPA2 data cipher, replacing the legacy TKIP/RC4 design.

**Why it works:** AES-CCMP provides strong confidentiality and integrity and is the standardised WPA2 cipher.

**Why the others don't work:**
- TKIP is retained only for compatibility and is deprecated
- RC4 with a small IV describes WEP
- 3DES is not used for 802.11 link encryption

skills: 2.3: Compare and contrast wireless security protocols and authentication methods.
questions.question:
A university wants each student to log in to campus Wi-Fi using their personal username and password rather than a shared PSK, with an authentication server centrally tracking and authorising access.

Which authentication framework should the network team deploy on the WPA2-Enterprise SSID?

choices.text: RADIUS as the back-end authentication server for 802.1X on the SSID.
choices.explanation: RADIUS is the standard AAA server for 802.1X enterprise wireless authentication.

choices.text: WPA2 Personal with a shared passphrase distributed to all students each semester.
choices.explanation: WPA2 Personal uses one PSK for everyone, not per-user credentials.

choices.text: Kerberos tickets exchanged directly between each laptop and the access point.
choices.explanation: Access points do not natively terminate Kerberos for Wi-Fi authentication.

choices.text: SAML assertions passed between the access point and the campus identity provider.
choices.explanation: SAML is for web SSO between browsers and applications, not 802.1X wireless.

questions.tip: Identify the AAA server commonly paired with 802.1X.
questions.explanation:
RADIUS is the standard AAA service used to authenticate per-user logins on WPA2/WPA3 Enterprise SSIDs via 802.1X.

**Why it works:** RADIUS validates the user's credentials and returns Accept/Reject to the access point, enabling per-user accounting and policy.

**Why the others don't work:**
- WPA2 Personal uses a single shared key
- Kerberos is not the wireless edge authentication protocol
- SAML is a web-federation standard, not for 802.1X

skills: 2.3: Compare and contrast wireless security protocols and authentication methods.
questions.question:
A network team needs an AAA protocol for administering Cisco switches and routers that separates authentication, authorisation, and accounting into distinct exchanges and fully encrypts the body of each packet over TCP.

Which protocol meets these requirements?

choices.text: TACACS+ running over TCP, which separates AAA functions and encrypts the entire payload.
choices.explanation: TACACS+ uses TCP, separates AAA, and encrypts the packet body, unlike RADIUS.

choices.text: RADIUS over UDP, which combines authentication and authorisation in one exchange.
choices.explanation: RADIUS combines authentication and authorisation and only encrypts the password attribute.

choices.text: Kerberos using the Authentication Server and Ticket Granting Server.
choices.explanation: Kerberos is a ticket-based SSO protocol, not an AAA device-admin protocol.

choices.text: SAML assertions exchanged with the network device console.
choices.explanation: SAML is used for browser-based federation, not for switch/router CLI authentication.

questions.tip: Look for the AAA protocol that runs on TCP and encrypts the whole packet.
questions.explanation:
TACACS+ runs over TCP, separates the three AAA functions, and encrypts the full packet body, making it well-suited to network device administration.

**Why it works:** Separating authorisation from authentication allows granular per-command control on routers and switches, and full-body encryption protects sensitive exchanges.

**Why the others don't work:**
- RADIUS uses UDP, combines auth/authz, and only encrypts the password attribute
- Kerberos is for domain SSO, not device CLI AAA
- SAML targets web SSO, not network-device administration

skills: 2.3: Compare and contrast wireless security protocols and authentication methods.
questions.question:
A consultancy is rolling out a new corporate Wi-Fi network. Security requires both strong encryption and per-user accountability beyond a single shared key, while remaining compatible with current Windows and macOS laptops.

Which TWO configuration choices satisfy these requirements?

choices.text: Use WPA2-Enterprise or WPA3-Enterprise with AES-CCMP as the data cipher.
choices.explanation: Enterprise mode supports per-user credentials, and AES-CCMP provides strong encryption.

choices.text: Authenticate users against a RADIUS server using 802.1X.
choices.explanation: 802.1X with RADIUS enables per-user logins and central policy on the wireless edge.

choices.text: Use WPA2-Personal with a long shared passphrase rotated quarterly.
choices.explanation: A shared passphrase does not provide per-user accountability.

choices.text: Enable WEP for backwards compatibility with older Wi-Fi adapters.
choices.explanation: WEP is broken and unacceptable for any modern deployment.

choices.text: Configure TKIP as the only cipher to maximise compatibility.
choices.explanation: TKIP is the legacy WPA cipher and is deprecated in favour of AES-CCMP.

questions.tip: Combine the protocol mode that supports per-user identity with the cipher considered current best practice.
questions.explanation:
WPA2/WPA3-Enterprise with AES-CCMP combined with 802.1X over RADIUS provides per-user identity and strong encryption.

**Why it works:** Enterprise mode delegates authentication to RADIUS, while AES-CCMP secures the link layer.

**Why the others don't work:**
- A shared passphrase removes per-user accountability
- WEP is broken
- TKIP is deprecated and weakens WPA2

skills: 2.3: Compare and contrast wireless security protocols and authentication methods.
questions.question: Match each wireless or authentication term to its accurate description.

choices.text: Wi-Fi security generation that introduced AES-CCMP as the recommended cipher
choices.explanation: WPA2 standardised AES-CCMP for 802.11 confidentiality and integrity.

choices.text: Wi-Fi security generation that uses SAE to resist offline PSK attacks
choices.explanation: WPA3 replaced the WPA2 handshake with SAE for stronger PSK protection.

choices.text: Legacy WPA cipher based on RC4 retained for backwards compatibility
choices.explanation: TKIP was the original WPA cipher and is deprecated under WPA2/WPA3.

choices.text: Ticket-based authentication protocol used in Active Directory domains
choices.explanation: Kerberos issues TGTs and service tickets within a domain realm.

questions.tip: Distinguish wireless cipher names from authentication frameworks.
questions.explanation: WPA2 and WPA3 are wireless security generations; TKIP is a cipher; Kerberos is an authentication framework used in domain environments.

skills: 2.4: Summarize types of malware and tools/methods for detection, removal, and prevention.
questions.question:
A small business reports that several spreadsheets on a shared drive now end with a strange extension and that a text file in each folder demands payment in cryptocurrency to recover the data. Backups have not been verified for weeks.

Which type of malware is described?

choices.text: Ransomware that encrypts user files and demands payment for the decryption key.
choices.explanation: Renamed files and a payment demand are the hallmark behaviour of ransomware.

choices.text: A keylogger silently capturing keystrokes from each affected workstation.
choices.explanation: Keyloggers do not rename files or demand payment; they harvest credentials quietly.

choices.text: A cryptominer using local CPU cycles to mine currency in the background.
choices.explanation: Cryptominers steal compute resources but do not encrypt user data or post ransom notes.

choices.text: Adware that injects pop-ups into the user's browser sessions.
choices.explanation: Adware targets browser experience and does not rename files or demand a payment.

questions.tip: Match the behaviour described to the malware whose business model relies on extortion.
questions.explanation:
Ransomware encrypts user files and posts a ransom note demanding payment for decryption.

**Why it works:** Renamed files with unusual extensions and an explicit payment demand are textbook ransomware indicators.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Keyloggers steal credentials silently and do not encrypt data
- Cryptominers consume CPU but leave files intact
- Adware focuses on advertising rather than extortion

skills: 2.4: Summarize types of malware and tools/methods for detection, removal, and prevention.
questions.question:
A forensic analyst is investigating a workstation that exhibits persistent suspicious behaviour even after a full antivirus scan and reboot. Hidden processes appear in memory snapshots but are invisible to Task Manager, and key system binaries appear to have been tampered with at a low level.

Which malware category best fits this profile?

choices.text: Rootkit operating at a privileged layer to hide processes and modify system binaries.
choices.explanation: Rootkits hook the OS at kernel or low level, hiding artefacts from standard tools.

choices.text: Trojan disguised as a legitimate application that the user installed willingly.
choices.explanation: A Trojan describes the delivery vector, not the persistence and hiding behaviour described.

choices.text: Boot sector virus that overwrites the MBR before the OS loads.
choices.explanation: Boot sector infection is a different persistence method and would not specifically hide live processes from Task Manager.

choices.text: Spyware that exfiltrates browsing history to a remote server.
choices.explanation: Spyware focuses on data theft and is not characterised by deep OS subversion.

questions.tip: Identify malware that subverts the OS to hide itself.
questions.explanation:
Rootkits operate at privileged levels to conceal processes and tamper with system files, matching the symptoms.

**Why it works:** Rootkit hooks intercept calls used by Task Manager and AV scanners, hiding malicious activity from user-mode tools.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Trojan refers to delivery, not the hiding behaviour
- Boot sector viruses target the MBR rather than runtime process hiding
- Spyware harvests data but does not deeply subvert the OS

skills: 2.4: Summarize types of malware and tools/methods for detection, removal, and prevention.
questions.question:
A security team wants centralised visibility across laptops, servers, and cloud workloads, with telemetry from each endpoint correlated and investigated by analysts. They need behavioural detection of suspicious activity rather than only signature matching.

Which tool category should they adopt?

choices.text: Endpoint detection and response (EDR) collecting telemetry and enabling behavioural investigation.
choices.explanation: EDR provides per-endpoint telemetry, behavioural detection, and analyst investigation tools.

choices.text: A signature-only antivirus product with daily definition updates.
choices.explanation: Signature-only AV lacks the behavioural detection and centralised investigation described.

choices.text: An email security gateway scanning inbound and outbound messages.
choices.explanation: Email gateways focus on message content, not endpoint telemetry.

choices.text: A software firewall blocking inbound TCP connections per host.
choices.explanation: Host firewalls control network traffic but do not provide behavioural endpoint investigation.

questions.tip: Look for the category whose name describes endpoint telemetry and behavioural response.
questions.explanation:
EDR is the category that collects per-endpoint telemetry, applies behavioural detection, and supports analyst investigation.

**Why it works:** Continuous telemetry plus behavioural analytics catches threats that signature AV misses, and analysts can pivot through the data.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Signature AV cannot do behavioural investigation
- Email gateways inspect messages, not endpoint activity
- Host firewalls filter traffic without analysing process behaviour

skills: 2.4: Summarize types of malware and tools/methods for detection, removal, and prevention.
questions.question:
A junior analyst has flagged a recent intrusion in which the malicious code never wrote a binary to disk. Instead, it executed entirely from within PowerShell and the Windows Management Instrumentation subsystem, leaving few file-based artefacts for traditional AV to scan.

Which malware classification best matches this technique?

choices.text: Fileless malware that lives in memory and abuses built-in scripting and management subsystems.
choices.explanation: Fileless malware avoids writing executables to disk and runs through native tools.

choices.text: Boot sector virus that overwrites the master boot record at startup.
choices.explanation: Boot sector viruses write to the MBR; they are not memory-only.

choices.text: Adware that injects banners into the user's browser sessions.
choices.explanation: Adware is a user-visible nuisance, not stealth in-memory execution.

choices.text: Stalkerware tracking the user's physical location over time.
choices.explanation: Stalkerware focuses on surveillance, not the on-disk versus in-memory distinction.

questions.tip: Identify the malware family that deliberately avoids writing artefacts to disk.
questions.explanation:
Fileless malware lives in memory and leverages built-in scripting frameworks, evading traditional file-based AV.

**Why it works:** Without a disk artefact, signature scanners have nothing to match, so detection requires behavioural monitoring.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Boot sector viruses do write to disk (the MBR)
- Adware is highly visible by design
- Stalkerware tracks users rather than describing a delivery technique

skills: 2.4: Summarize types of malware and tools/methods for detection, removal, and prevention.
questions.question:
Following a phishing campaign that snared three users in the marketing team, the security manager wants to reduce both the likelihood and impact of similar incidents. Budget allows for two complementary controls focused on prevention and human factors.

Which TWO actions should the manager prioritise?

choices.text: Deploy an email security gateway to filter malicious links and attachments before delivery.
choices.explanation: Gateway filtering removes much of the malicious mail before it reaches inboxes.

choices.text: Run regular antiphishing training and simulated phishing exercises for staff.
choices.explanation: User education addresses the human factor the gateway cannot fully cover.

choices.text: Disable Windows Update on all marketing laptops to avoid disrupting users.
choices.explanation: Disabling updates increases exposure to known vulnerabilities.

choices.text: Add the marketing team to the local Administrators group on their laptops.
choices.explanation: Local admin rights amplify the damage from a successful phishing payload.

choices.text: Replace MFA with single-factor login to reduce login friction.
choices.explanation: Removing MFA increases the success rate of credential phishing.

questions.tip: Pair a technical control with a control aimed at human behaviour.
questions.explanation:
Combining an email security gateway with antiphishing user training tackles both the technical and human sides of the attack.

**Why it works:** The gateway blocks most malicious messages; training reduces the impact of those that get through.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Turning off updates raises exposure
- Granting local admin amplifies payload impact
- Removing MFA makes credential theft far more damaging

skills: 2.4: Summarize types of malware and tools/methods for detection, removal, and prevention.
questions.question: Match each malware type to its primary behaviour.

choices.text: Disguises itself as a legitimate program to trick the user into installing it
choices.explanation: A Trojan relies on social engineering of the installer.

choices.text: Silently collects information about the user's activity and sends it to an attacker
choices.explanation: Spyware focuses on covert data collection.

choices.text: Captures every keystroke the user types and forwards it for credential harvesting
choices.explanation: Keyloggers record input to steal credentials and messages.

choices.text: Hijacks CPU or GPU cycles on the host to mine cryptocurrency for the attacker
choices.explanation: Cryptominers monetise stolen compute time.

questions.tip: Match each malware to the resource or asset it primarily targets.
questions.explanation: Each malware type has a distinct goal, from credential theft to compute abuse to covert installation.

skills: 2.5: Compare and contrast common social engineering attacks, threats, and vulnerabilities.
questions.question:
The finance director receives a phone call from someone claiming to be a senior IT engineer who urgently needs her network password to clear a payroll backlog before close of business. The caller spoofs the internal helpdesk caller ID and pressures her to comply.

Which attack technique is being used?

choices.text: Vishing, a voice-based phishing call that pressures the target into revealing credentials.
choices.explanation: Vishing is phishing conducted by phone, often with caller ID spoofing and authority pressure.

choices.text: Smishing using SMS messages to lure the target to a credential page.
choices.explanation: Smishing is SMS-based, not a voice call.

choices.text: QR code phishing that redirects the target to a fake login portal.
choices.explanation: There is no QR code in the scenario; this is a voice call.

choices.text: Tailgating to follow an authorised employee through a controlled door.
choices.explanation: Tailgating is a physical entry technique, not a phone-based social engineering call.

questions.tip: Identify the channel the social engineer is using.
questions.explanation:
A spoofed voice call pressuring the target for credentials is vishing.

**Why it works:** Caller ID spoofing creates apparent authority and urgency motivates the target to skip verification.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Smishing uses SMS
- QR code phishing relies on a scanned code
- Tailgating involves physical premises

skills: 2.5: Compare and contrast common social engineering attacks, threats, and vulnerabilities.
questions.question:
Customers connecting to a coffee shop's public Wi-Fi are unknowingly associating with a rogue access point that mimics the shop's SSID with a stronger signal. The attacker then intercepts traffic and harvests session cookies.

Which attack does this describe?

choices.text: Evil twin, a rogue AP that impersonates a legitimate SSID to intercept client traffic.
choices.explanation: An evil twin advertises the same SSID and lures clients to associate, enabling interception.

choices.text: Distributed denial of service against the coffee shop's wireless network.
choices.explanation: A DDoS would disrupt service, not silently intercept traffic.

choices.text: SQL injection against the coffee shop's loyalty website.
choices.explanation: SQL injection targets a web app's database, not Wi-Fi clients.

choices.text: Dictionary attack against the shop's WPA2 pre-shared key.
choices.explanation: A dictionary attack guesses passwords offline; it does not impersonate an SSID.

questions.tip: Identify the wireless attack that involves a fake AP with the same SSID.
questions.explanation:
An evil twin is a rogue AP that mimics a legitimate SSID to capture client traffic.

**Why it works:** Clients pick the strongest signal for a known SSID; once associated, the attacker can inspect or modify traffic.

**Why the others don't work:**
- DDoS is disruption, not interception
- SQL injection targets a database
- Dictionary attack focuses on cracking, not impersonation

skills: 2.5: Compare and contrast common social engineering attacks, threats, and vulnerabilities.
questions.question:
Following initial reconnaissance, a junior analyst notices a public-facing search form that returns database error messages when special characters are entered. Crafted input causes the application to reveal data from tables the user should not be able to access.

Which attack class is being exploited?

choices.text: SQL injection against the search form's database query.
choices.explanation: Special characters that change the query structure and leak data indicate SQL injection.

choices.text: Cross-site scripting in the search form's rendered output.
choices.explanation: XSS executes script in the victim's browser; it does not directly leak DB tables to the requester.

choices.text: Distributed denial of service overwhelming the application server.
choices.explanation: DDoS denies service; it does not exfiltrate database rows.

choices.text: On-path attack intercepting traffic between client and server.
choices.explanation: An on-path attack would require the attacker to sit between two endpoints, not just submit a form.

questions.tip: Special characters that change a database query point to one specific class.
questions.explanation:
Database error messages and data leakage from crafted input are signatures of SQL injection.

**Why it works:** Untrusted input is concatenated into the SQL query, allowing the attacker to alter its logic and read unauthorised tables.

**Why the others don't work:**
- XSS runs in the browser, not the database
- DDoS denies service rather than exfiltrating data
- On-path requires positioning between client and server

skills: 2.5: Compare and contrast common social engineering attacks, threats, and vulnerabilities.
questions.question:
The CFO of a manufacturing firm receives a convincing email that appears to come from the CEO, instructing her to wire a large sum to a new supplier account before the end of the quarter. The email originates from a lookalike domain, and the CEO is on holiday.

Which threat does this describe?

choices.text: Business email compromise impersonating an executive to authorise a fraudulent transfer.
choices.explanation: BEC targets a finance decision-maker by impersonating an executive to redirect funds.

choices.text: Smishing using SMS messages to harvest banking credentials.
choices.explanation: The attack arrives by email, not SMS.

choices.text: Tailgating into the finance office to obtain a paper invoice.
choices.explanation: There is no physical entry component in the scenario.

choices.text: Cross-site scripting targeting the firm's accounting web portal.
choices.explanation: XSS is a web vulnerability and is not what is described.

questions.tip: Identify the email-based fraud that targets executive payment authority.
questions.explanation:
An impersonated executive email pressuring a finance officer to wire funds is the textbook description of BEC.

**Why it works:** The lookalike domain and the CEO's absence support social pressure to bypass normal payment controls.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Smishing requires SMS
- Tailgating is physical
- XSS targets web applications, not the wire transfer process

skills: 2.5: Compare and contrast common social engineering attacks, threats, and vulnerabilities.
questions.question:
During a vulnerability review, the security team has flagged several systemic weaknesses across the estate that materially increase the likelihood of malware infection if not addressed. Leadership has asked for the TWO most impactful classes of weakness to remediate first.

Which TWO should the team prioritise?

choices.text: Unpatched systems missing critical OS and application updates.
choices.explanation: Unpatched systems are routinely exploited by commodity and targeted malware.

choices.text: Unprotected systems missing antivirus or with the host firewall disabled.
choices.explanation: Endpoints without basic protections are easy targets for known threats.

choices.text: Workstations that have an active screensaver lock policy.
choices.explanation: Screensaver locks are a security control, not a vulnerability.

choices.text: Users authenticating with MFA on their corporate accounts.
choices.explanation: MFA reduces risk; it is not a vulnerability.

choices.text: A daily verified backup process with offsite retention.
choices.explanation: Verified backups improve recovery posture and are not a vulnerability.

questions.tip: Identify the two states that materially raise the chance of compromise.
questions.explanation:
Unpatched and unprotected systems are the foundational weaknesses that allow malware to land and persist.

**Why it works:** Patching closes known exploits, and basic AV/firewall coverage blocks routine threats; both directly lower the likelihood of compromise.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Screensaver locks, MFA, and verified backups are positive controls, not weaknesses

skills: 2.5: Compare and contrast common social engineering attacks, threats, and vulnerabilities.
questions.question: Match each social engineering or threat technique to its accurate description.

choices.text: Targeted phishing crafted for a specific individual or small group
choices.explanation: Spear phishing tailors the lure with personal context.

choices.text: Phishing aimed specifically at very high-value executive targets
choices.explanation: Whaling targets the biggest fish such as the CEO or CFO.

choices.text: Observing a target entering credentials or PII over their shoulder
choices.explanation: Shoulder surfing relies on physical proximity and line of sight.

choices.text: Retrieving discarded paper or media to find sensitive information
choices.explanation: Dumpster diving harvests improperly disposed-of records.

questions.tip: Distinguish targeted email attacks from physical-world reconnaissance methods.
questions.explanation: Each technique uses a different channel or audience to gather information or compromise a target.

skills: 2.6: Given a scenario, implement procedures for basic small office/home office (SOHO) malware removal.
questions.question:
A technician at a small accountancy firm has just confirmed that a laptop is exhibiting clear ransomware symptoms. Before doing anything else, he wants to prevent the infection from spreading to the file share the laptop has mapped.

Which step should the technician take FIRST?

choices.text: Quarantine the infected system by disconnecting it from the network.
choices.explanation: Isolation prevents lateral spread before any remediation begins.

choices.text: Reimage the laptop from the standard build before any other action.
choices.explanation: Reimaging comes later in the process, after isolation and investigation.

choices.text: Educate the end user on safer browsing habits.
choices.explanation: End-user education is the final step in the process, not the immediate response.

choices.text: Enable System Restore and create a restore point on the infected laptop.
choices.explanation: System Restore should be disabled, not enabled, during remediation in Windows Home.

questions.tip: Think about what must be done before any cleaning or recovery to contain the threat.
questions.explanation:
Quarantining the infected system by removing it from the network is the immediate containment step after symptom verification.

**Why it works:** Isolation prevents the malware from reaching shares, peers, and the rest of the environment while investigation continues.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Reimaging belongs to the remediation phase
- User education is the final step
- Enabling System Restore during infection can persist the malware

skills: 2.6: Given a scenario, implement procedures for basic small office/home office (SOHO) malware removal.
questions.question:
After isolating a malware-infected Windows Home PC, the technician wants to prevent the malware from being captured inside an automatic snapshot that could be unwittingly reapplied later.

Which action addresses this concern?

choices.text: Disable System Restore on the infected PC before remediation.
choices.explanation: Disabling System Restore clears existing infected snapshots and prevents new ones.

choices.text: Enable System Restore and create a new restore point immediately.
choices.explanation: Creating a restore point now would snapshot the malware itself.

choices.text: Run Windows Update to install the latest cumulative update.
choices.explanation: Updates do not address malicious restore points.

choices.text: Clear the browser cache through the user's default web browser.
choices.explanation: Clearing browser cache does not impact System Restore snapshots.

questions.tip: Think about why a restore point could re-infect the system.
questions.explanation:
Disabling System Restore in Windows Home removes the infected snapshots that could otherwise reintroduce the malware.

**Why it works:** Restore points can preserve a copy of malicious files; disabling the feature clears the slate before cleaning begins.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Creating a restore point now captures the malware
- Patching is unrelated to restore-point cleanliness
- Browser cache does not interact with System Restore

skills: 2.6: Given a scenario, implement procedures for basic small office/home office (SOHO) malware removal.
questions.question:
A technician needs to scan a heavily infected workstation whose malware injects itself into normal Windows services, defeating attempts to remove it while the OS is fully running.

Which scanning approach gives the best chance of removing the threat?

choices.text: Boot into Safe Mode or a preinstallation environment and scan from there.
choices.explanation: Safe Mode/PE prevents most malware from loading, so scanners can access infected files.

choices.text: Run a full scan while all normal services and user apps are running.
choices.explanation: Active malware can block or evade scans run from a fully booted session.

choices.text: Schedule a scan to run overnight while the user remains logged in.
choices.explanation: Scheduling does not address the loaded malware interfering with the scan.

choices.text: Disable all networking and run the scan from the user's normal desktop session.
choices.explanation: Containment is good, but the malware is still loaded and can interfere with the scan.

questions.tip: Consider an environment where most malicious code is not loaded.
questions.explanation:
Running scans from Safe Mode or a Windows preinstallation environment keeps the malware unloaded so it cannot defend itself.

**Why it works:** Without the malicious processes running, scanners can access and clean infected files reliably.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Active sessions allow malware to interfere
- Scheduling does not change the runtime state
- Disabling networking is helpful but does not unload the malware

skills: 2.6: Given a scenario, implement procedures for basic small office/home office (SOHO) malware removal.
questions.question:
The cleanup of a SOHO PC is nearly complete. Anti-malware definitions are current, scheduled scans are configured, and a clean restore point has been created. The technician now wants to reduce the chance of the user re-infecting the machine through the same vector.

Which action best closes out the engagement?

choices.text: Educate the end user about the specific lure and safer habits going forward.
choices.explanation: User education is the final step and directly addresses recurrence.

choices.text: Disable System Restore again as a precaution after handing the laptop back.
choices.explanation: System Restore should remain enabled after a clean restore point is created.

choices.text: Disconnect the laptop from the network permanently for safety.
choices.explanation: Permanent disconnection is not practical and not part of the process.

choices.text: Remove the anti-malware software now that the system is clean.
choices.explanation: Removing AV after cleanup eliminates ongoing protection.

questions.tip: Identify the last step of the SOHO malware removal process.
questions.explanation:
Educating the end user is the final step of the SOHO malware removal process and reduces recurrence.

**Why it works:** Most reinfections come from the same behaviour; teaching the user what to look for closes the loop.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Disabling System Restore again undoes step 9
- Permanent disconnection is impractical
- Removing AV leaves the system unprotected

skills: 2.6: Given a scenario, implement procedures for basic small office/home office (SOHO) malware removal.
questions.question:
After remediating an infected PC, the technician wants to harden the system against the same family of malware reappearing. The end user is non-technical and will not perform any manual maintenance.

Which TWO actions should the technician configure before returning the machine?

choices.text: Schedule regular full anti-malware scans on the workstation.
choices.explanation: Automated scans catch new threats without relying on the user.

choices.text: Enable automatic updates for the anti-malware software and OS.
choices.explanation: Automatic updates keep signatures and patches current without user intervention.

choices.text: Disable the host firewall to reduce performance overhead.
choices.explanation: Disabling the firewall removes a critical control.

choices.text: Add the end user to the local Administrators group to ease future tasks.
choices.explanation: Local admin rights make future infections more damaging.

choices.text: Remove all anti-malware software once a clean reimage is complete.
choices.explanation: The PC needs ongoing protection, not removal of AV.

questions.tip: Combine automation that runs without the user thinking about it.
questions.explanation:
Scheduled scans plus automatic updates for AV and OS give ongoing protection without relying on the user.

**Why it works:** Both steps run unattended and address detection of new threats and closure of patched vulnerabilities.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Disabling the firewall weakens defence
- Granting local admin increases blast radius
- Removing AV leaves the system unprotected

skills: 2.6: Given a scenario, implement procedures for basic small office/home office (SOHO) malware removal.
questions.question: Arrange the following SOHO malware removal steps in the correct order according to CompTIA's recommended best practice procedure.

choices.text: Investigate and verify the malware symptoms on the affected system
choices.explanation: Confirming the infection precedes any containment or remediation.

choices.text: Quarantine the infected system by disconnecting it from the network
choices.explanation: Isolation prevents the malware from spreading during the rest of the process.

choices.text: Disable System Restore on Windows Home systems
choices.explanation: Disabling System Restore removes infected snapshots before cleaning.

choices.text: Remediate the infected system by updating anti-malware definitions and scanning with appropriate techniques such as Safe Mode
choices.explanation: Updated AV plus an offline-style scan removes the malware.

choices.text: Schedule scans, enable updates, re-enable System Restore, and create a clean restore point
choices.explanation: Post-cleaning hardening puts the machine into a safer ongoing state.

choices.text: Educate the end user about the threat and safer practices
choices.explanation: Education is the final step to reduce recurrence.

questions.tip: Containment comes before cleaning, and education comes last.
questions.explanation: The SOHO removal process moves from verification through containment, remediation, and post-cleanup hardening before closing with end-user education.

skills: 2.7: Given a scenario, apply workstation security options and hardening techniques.
questions.question:
A travelling consultant frequently leaves her laptop unattended at airport tables for short periods. The IT team wants to ensure that a brief walk-away does not expose her open documents, without relying on her to remember to lock the screen.

Which workstation hardening option directly addresses this risk?

choices.text: Configure a screensaver lock that triggers after a short idle timeout.
choices.explanation: An idle-based screensaver lock secures the session automatically when the user steps away.

choices.text: Enable AutoRun for removable drives to speed up workflows.
choices.explanation: AutoRun is a known malware vector and should be disabled, not enabled.

choices.text: Add the user account to the local Administrators group.
choices.explanation: Local admin rights do not prevent walk-up access to an unlocked screen.

choices.text: Shorten the password expiration to seven days.
choices.explanation: Frequent password changes do not stop someone using an unlocked session.

questions.tip: Look for the control that secures an unattended session automatically.
questions.explanation:
An idle-triggered screensaver lock secures the session even when the user forgets, directly addressing brief walk-aways.

**Why it works:** The OS locks automatically after the configured timeout, requiring re-authentication on return.

**Why the others don't work:**
- AutoRun is a malware vector
- Local admin does not affect session locking
- Short password expiry does not prevent walk-up access

skills: 2.7: Given a scenario, apply workstation security options and hardening techniques.
questions.question:
An auditor flags that several workstations still use the default Administrator account name with no password set in BIOS/UEFI. The IT lead wants to address both the firmware-level and OS-level risk.

Which pair of hardening steps satisfies the auditor's concern?

choices.text: Rename and password-protect the default OS administrator account, and set a BIOS/UEFI supervisor password.
choices.explanation: Both layers are hardened, removing easy guesswork on the default admin and firmware access.

choices.text: Disable Windows Defender and rely on a single set of firmware credentials.
choices.explanation: Disabling Defender weakens the OS, and a single firmware password does not address the OS account.

choices.text: Add the default administrator to the Guests group to limit its rights.
choices.explanation: The default administrator cannot effectively be downgraded that way and the firmware risk remains.

choices.text: Enable AutoRun on removable media and require a BIOS password.
choices.explanation: AutoRun is a known malware vector and should be disabled, not enabled.

questions.tip: Look for the option that addresses both firmware and OS administrator hygiene.
questions.explanation:
Renaming and password-protecting the OS administrator account and setting a BIOS/UEFI supervisor password covers both layers raised by the audit.

**Why it works:** The default identity is removed at the OS layer, and firmware-level changes are gated behind a password.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Disabling Defender weakens the OS
- The default administrator cannot simply be moved to Guests
- Enabling AutoRun introduces a known malware vector

skills: 2.7: Given a scenario, apply workstation security options and hardening techniques.
questions.question:
A user has set her password to her child's name with a single capital letter. The security team is rolling out a stronger password standard that combines length, character variety, and uniqueness across systems.

Which requirement set best reflects modern password considerations?

choices.text: A minimum length, a mix of character types, uniqueness from prior passwords, and avoidance of dictionary words.
choices.explanation: Length, complexity, uniqueness, and avoiding common words capture the standard considerations.

choices.text: A short fixed-length password rotated every two days.
choices.explanation: Short passwords with constant rotation lead to weak, predictable patterns.

choices.text: Allowing the same password across all corporate and personal accounts for simplicity.
choices.explanation: Password reuse drastically amplifies breach impact.

choices.text: Disabling MFA so users only need to remember the password.
choices.explanation: Disabling MFA weakens authentication and is unrelated to password strength criteria.

questions.tip: Identify the combination of factors that defines password strength and resistance to reuse.
questions.explanation:
A minimum length, character-type mix, uniqueness across systems, and avoidance of dictionary words covers modern password considerations.

**Why it works:** Each factor independently raises the difficulty of guessing or cracking the password.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Very short, constantly rotated passwords produce predictable patterns
- Reuse across accounts magnifies any breach
- Disabling MFA weakens authentication overall

skills: 2.7: Given a scenario, apply workstation security options and hardening techniques.
questions.question:
A technician is hardening a public reception PC used to look up appointments. He wants to reduce brute-force risk against any local accounts and ensure the system does not run unnecessary background services that could be exploited.

Which two-part configuration should he apply?

choices.text: Enable failed-attempt account lockout and disable services that are not required.
choices.explanation: Lockout slows brute force and disabling unused services shrinks the attack surface.

choices.text: Enable AutoRun for the reception kiosk and set passwords never to expire.
choices.explanation: AutoRun is a malware vector and non-expiring passwords reduce account hygiene.

choices.text: Add the reception user to the local Administrators group and enable Guest.
choices.explanation: Granting admin rights and enabling Guest both expand attack surface.

choices.text: Disable the screensaver lock so the kiosk remains responsive at all times.
choices.explanation: Disabling the lock leaves the session open to anyone walking by.

questions.tip: Combine a control that limits guessing attempts with one that shrinks attack surface.
questions.explanation:
Enabling failed-attempt lockout plus disabling unused services tackles both brute force and exposed surface.

**Why it works:** Lockout caps password-guessing attempts, and removing unneeded services eliminates exploitable code paths.

**Why the others don't work:**
- AutoRun and never-expiring passwords weaken hardening
- Local admin plus Guest enabled increases exposure
- Disabling the screensaver lock removes a key kiosk control

skills: 2.7: Given a scenario, apply workstation security options and hardening techniques.
questions.question:
A technician is preparing a new contractor's laptop. Account management policy requires that the account is only valid for the contract window and that the Guest account is not available.

Which TWO settings should the technician apply?

choices.text: Set an account expiration date matching the end of the contract.
choices.explanation: Expiration disables the account automatically when the contract ends.

choices.text: Disable the built-in Guest account on the laptop.
choices.explanation: Disabling Guest removes an unauthenticated path to the system.

choices.text: Set the password never to expire to avoid helpdesk calls.
choices.explanation: Non-expiring passwords undermine account hygiene.

choices.text: Add the contractor account to the local Administrators group.
choices.explanation: Default admin rights for a contractor breaks least privilege.

choices.text: Disable failed-attempt lockout to keep the contractor productive.
choices.explanation: Disabling lockout makes brute force trivial.

questions.tip: Match each policy requirement to a specific account setting.
questions.explanation:
Setting an expiration date and disabling the Guest account map directly to the policy requirements.

**Why it works:** Expiration handles the temporary nature of the role automatically, and disabling Guest removes an unauthenticated entry path.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Non-expiring passwords weaken hygiene
- Local admin defeats least privilege
- Disabling lockout enables brute-force attacks

skills: 2.7: Given a scenario, apply workstation security options and hardening techniques.
questions.question: Match each workstation hardening technique to the risk it primarily mitigates.

choices.text: Protects stored data if the device is lost or the drive is removed
choices.explanation: Full-volume encryption keeps offline data unreadable without the key.

choices.text: Prevents removable media from launching code automatically when inserted

choices.text: Stops unauthorised users from changing firmware settings or boot order

questions.explanation: Each hardening technique addresses a different layer of risk on the workstation.

skills: 2.8: Given a scenario, apply common methods for securing mobile devices.
questions.question:
A sales rep's company iPhone is reported missing after a conference. The data on it includes signed contracts and customer contact lists. The IT lead has central management enrolled for every corporate device.

Which action best protects the organisation's data?

choices.text: Issue a remote wipe through the MDM console.
choices.explanation: Remote wipe removes corporate data before the device falls into the wrong hands.

choices.text: Lower the failed-login attempt limit to extend the lockout window.
choices.explanation: Adjusting a single setting after loss does not protect data already on the device.

choices.text: Disable encryption on the lost device to ease recovery.
choices.explanation: Disabling encryption would expose data; encryption protects it.

choices.text: Wait 72 hours before acting in case the device is found.
choices.explanation: Delaying response gives an attacker more time to extract data.

questions.tip: Pick the MDM action that immediately neutralises stored corporate data.
questions.explanation:
A remote wipe through MDM removes corporate data from the device, protecting it from whoever has it now.

**Why it works:** The wipe is authoritative, fast, and centrally controlled, removing the sensitive material before exploitation.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Lockout adjustments do not address data already on the device
- Disabling encryption exposes data rather than protecting it
- Waiting prolongs the window of risk

skills: 2.8: Given a scenario, apply common methods for securing mobile devices.
questions.question:
A school's mobile policy requires that every student tablet enforces a screen lock that uses something biometric the student can use one-handed while carrying books, but pattern locks are not acceptable because they leave smudge traces.

Which screen lock method best satisfies the policy?

choices.text: Fingerprint unlock using the device's built-in sensor.
choices.explanation: Fingerprint is biometric, fast, one-handed, and avoids smudge patterns.

choices.text: Pattern unlock using a memorable shape on the grid.
choices.explanation: Pattern unlock is explicitly excluded by the policy because of smudge traces.

choices.text: Swipe to unlock with no credential challenge.
choices.explanation: Swipe is not a real lock and provides no authentication.

choices.text: A six-digit PIN entered with both hands on a virtual keypad.
choices.explanation: A PIN works, but it is not biometric and the policy specifies biometric one-handed use.

questions.tip: Re-read the constraints in the policy carefully.
questions.explanation:
Fingerprint unlock is biometric, suitable for one-handed use, and does not leave a recoverable pattern.

**Why it works:** A fingerprint sensor authenticates on contact, satisfies the biometric requirement, and works with a single hand.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Pattern is excluded
- Swipe provides no authentication
- A PIN is not biometric

skills: 2.8: Given a scenario, apply common methods for securing mobile devices.
questions.question:
A field engineer reports that her Android phone has been showing pop-up adverts shortly after she installed a flashlight utility from a third-party APK site. The IT team wants to ensure the device receives current security fixes and removes any malicious payload.

Which two-part approach is appropriate?

choices.text: Run an endpoint anti-malware scan and apply pending OS and application updates.
choices.explanation: Anti-malware addresses the payload and patches close the original entry vector.

choices.text: Disable encryption on the device to allow the scan to inspect more files.
choices.explanation: Disabling encryption is unnecessary and weakens protection.

choices.text: Sideload additional APKs from the same site to overwrite the flashlight app.
choices.explanation: Trusting more APKs from an untrusted source compounds the risk.

choices.text: Turn off the screen lock to make further scanning easier for the user.
choices.explanation: Removing the lock weakens overall device security.

questions.tip: Pair a control that removes the malware with one that closes the vulnerability.
questions.explanation:
Running an anti-malware scan together with applying OS and application updates handles both the payload and the vulnerability that allowed it in.

**Why it works:** The scan cleans the device while patching closes the underlying vector and reduces future risk.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Disabling encryption is unnecessary and weakens protection
- Adding more sideloaded APKs increases exposure
- Removing the screen lock weakens security

skills: 2.8: Given a scenario, apply common methods for securing mobile devices.
questions.question:
A user's iPad has been left in a taxi. The user wants to see roughly where the device currently is so they can decide whether to retrieve it or invoke a remote wipe.

Which category of mobile security feature should they use?

choices.text: A locator application that reports the device's current location.
choices.explanation: Locator services provide the live position the user needs.

choices.text: A remote backup application that uploads photos to cloud storage.
choices.explanation: Backups preserve data but do not show the device location.

choices.text: Content filtering that blocks adult websites on the device's browser.
choices.explanation: Content filtering controls what is loaded, not where the device is.

choices.text: An antivirus app scanning installed packages for known threats.
choices.explanation: Antivirus does not provide location information.

questions.tip: Choose the feature whose name describes its purpose for lost devices.
questions.explanation:
Locator applications report the device's current position so the user can decide whether to recover or wipe.

**Why it works:** Location services on mobile platforms surface a map of the device's last known position to the owner.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Backups preserve data but not whereabouts
- Content filtering targets browsing behaviour
- Antivirus scans for malware, not location

skills: 2.8: Given a scenario, apply common methods for securing mobile devices.
questions.question:
The security team is launching a BYOD programme. Personal devices will be allowed to access corporate email and a corporate VPN, but the team must enforce baseline corporate security on those devices.

Which TWO controls should the team implement?

choices.text: Enrol BYOD devices in an MDM platform that applies a corporate profile.
choices.explanation: MDM enrolment is the foundation for enforcing corporate baselines on personal devices.

choices.text: Require device encryption and a screen lock as part of the corporate profile.
choices.explanation: Encryption and a screen lock protect corporate data at rest on personal hardware.

choices.text: Disable patching on BYOD devices to avoid disrupting the user.
choices.explanation: Disabling patching increases exposure to known vulnerabilities.

choices.text: Block all locator applications because they collect personal data.
choices.explanation: Locator features are part of recovering lost corporate-enrolled devices.

choices.text: Allow indefinite failed-login attempts so users are never locked out.
choices.explanation: Removing failed-attempt limits enables brute force.

questions.tip: Pair enrolment with the baseline protections it should enforce.
questions.explanation:
MDM enrolment with a profile mandating encryption and a screen lock is the BYOD baseline.

**Why it works:** The MDM platform centrally enforces the corporate posture, and encryption plus lock protect data on the user's device.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Disabling patching weakens hardening
- Disabling locators removes recovery capability
- Removing login limits enables brute force

skills: 2.8: Given a scenario, apply common methods for securing mobile devices.
questions.question: Match each mobile security capability to its primary purpose.

choices.text: Erases corporate or all device data when the device is lost or stolen

choices.text: Preserves user data offsite so it can be recovered after a wipe or replacement

choices.text: Centrally applies settings such as VPN, Wi-Fi, and security policies to a device

choices.text: Locks or wipes the device after a set number of incorrect unlock attempts
